topics.UNW: 5R approach for smokers unwilling to quit

cards.q: According to WHO, how many deaths does tobacco cause each year worldwide, and how many are from second-hand smoke?
cards.a:
• About **8 million deaths per year** from tobacco
• **Over 1 million** of these are non-smokers exposed to **second-hand smoke**
• Up to half of long-term users die from a tobacco-related disease
cards.m: 8 million a year = roughly one tobacco death every 4 seconds.

cards.q: What proportion of all cancer deaths globally is attributed to tobacco use?
cards.a:
• **25%** (one in four) of all cancer deaths globally (WHO)
• Non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke are also at risk of **lung cancer**
cards.m: One in four cancer deaths has a cigarette behind it.

cards.q: What are the main adult health risks of second-hand smoke exposure in non-smokers?
cards.a:
• **Lung cancer** in never-smokers (WHO slide fact)
• Coronary heart disease and stroke
• Contributes to the **>1 million** annual deaths from second-hand smoke
• There is **no safe level** of exposure – ventilation and opening windows do not remove the risk
cards.m: Second-hand smoke: the non-smoker pays the smoker's bill.

cards.q: What was the prevalence of current smoking among Malaysian adults in NHMS 2019?
cards.a:
• **21.3%** of Malaysians aged **15 years and above** were current smokers
• About **4.8 million** people
cards.m: NHMS 2019: 21.3% ≈ one in five adults, 4.8 million smokers.

cards.q: How does smoking prevalence differ between Malaysian men and women (NHMS 2019)?
cards.a:
• **Male 40.5%** vs **female 1.2%**
• Smoking in Malaysia is overwhelmingly a male behaviour – ask every adult man about tobacco use at every visit
• Still ask women: low prevalence does not mean zero, and pregnancy makes it high-stakes
cards.m: Men 40, women 1 – about 2 in 5 Malaysian men smoke.

cards.q: What was the adult smoking prevalence in Malaysia in NHMS 2023, and how does it compare with 2019?
cards.a:
• NHMS 2023: about **19%** of adults are smokers
• Down from **21.3%** in NHMS 2019 – a slow fall, so most smokers remain untreated

cards.q: What proportion of current Malaysian smokers attempted to quit in the past 12 months (NHMS 2019), and what is the clinical implication?
cards.a:
• **Less than half** of current smokers made a quit attempt in the last 12 months
• Implication: clinicians must **ask and advise opportunistically** at every consultation rather than wait for the patient to raise it
cards.m: Most smokers will not walk in asking – every contact counts.

cards.q: What is the greatest preventable cause of death, and which component of tobacco causes addiction?
cards.a:
• **Tobacco use** is the greatest preventable cause of death
• **Nicotine** is the drug in tobacco that causes **addiction**
• Disease is caused mainly by the other components (tar, carbon monoxide, toxins), not nicotine
cards.m: People smoke for the nicotine but die from the tar and CO.

cards.q: What are the three main harmful components of cigarette smoke and what does each do?
cards.a:
• **Nicotine** – addiction; sympathetic stimulation
• **Tar** – contains carcinogens (e.g. polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines) → cancers, airway damage
• **Carbon monoxide** – binds haemoglobin → reduced oxygen delivery, cardiovascular damage
• Smoke contains about **7,000 chemicals**, at least **70 known carcinogens**
cards.m: N-T-C: Nicotine hooks, Tar cancers, CO chokes.

cards.q: Name some toxic chemicals in cigarette smoke with everyday comparisons useful when counselling patients.
cards.a:
• **Ammonia** – toilet cleaner
• **Formaldehyde** – used to preserve dead bodies
• **Arsenic** – rat poison
• **Hydrogen cyanide** – poison gas
• **Cadmium** – batteries; **acetone** – nail polish remover
• **Carbon monoxide** – car exhaust; **polonium-210** – radioactive
cards.m: 'You would not drink toilet cleaner or rat poison – why inhale them 20 times a day?'

cards.q: How does carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke harm the body?
cards.a:
• CO binds haemoglobin with about **200–250 times** the affinity of oxygen → **carboxyhaemoglobin**
• Reduces oxygen delivery → tissue hypoxia, extra cardiac work
• Damages endothelium → atherosclerosis
• Chronic hypoxia → **secondary polycythaemia**
• Pulse oximetry over-reads because it cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin
cards.m: CO is a seat-stealer: it sits on haemoglobin's oxygen seat and will not get up.

cards.q: Since when has Malaysia been a party to the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC)?
cards.a:
• Since **2005**
• The WHO FCTC uses the **MPOWER** package of measures for tobacco control and cessation

cards.q: What does each letter of the WHO MPOWER package stand for?
cards.a:
• **M** – Monitor tobacco use and prevention policies
• **P** – Protect people from **tobacco smoke**
• **O** – Offer help to quit tobacco use
• **W** – Warn about the dangers of tobacco
• **E** – Enforce bans on tobacco advertising, promotion and sponsorship
• **R** – Raise taxes on tobacco
• Note: slide p8 says 'Protect people from tobacco use'; the WHO wording is 'from tobacco **smoke**'
cards.m: MPOWER: Monitor, Protect, Offer, Warn, Enforce, Raise taxes.

cards.q: Which MPOWER component are healthcare providers responsible for?
cards.a:
• **O – Offer help to quit** tobacco use
• Delivered through brief intervention (5A/3A/ABC), quit clinics and pharmacotherapy
cards.m: Doctors hold the 'O' – the Offer.

cards.q: Within MPOWER, what do the 'E' and 'R' measures involve, and why is 'R' important?
cards.a:
• **E** – Enforce bans on tobacco advertising, promotion and sponsorship
• **R** – Raise taxes on tobacco
• Tax increases are one of the **most effective** population measures, especially for price-sensitive young people and low-income smokers
cards.m: Price up, packs down.

cards.q: How do you calculate pack-years? Work out Mr Ali's exposure (30 sticks/day for 30 years).
cards.a:
• **Pack-years = (sticks per day ÷ 20) × years smoked**
• Mr Ali: (30 ÷ 20) × 30 = **45 pack-years**
• Used to quantify cumulative risk (e.g. COPD, lung cancer)
cards.m: One pack = 20 sticks; one pack a day for one year = 1 pack-year.

cards.q: What are the main categories of smoking-related disease?
cards.a:
• **Cardiovascular** – coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease, aortic aneurysm
• **Respiratory** – COPD, lung cancer, asthma exacerbations, TB
• **Cancers** – many sites beyond the lung
• **Reproductive** – infertility, erectile dysfunction, pregnancy complications
• **Others** – diabetes, osteoporosis, cataract, periodontal disease, poor wound healing
cards.m: Smoking harms almost every organ – head (stroke) to toe (gangrene).

cards.q: Which cancers are causally linked to smoking?
cards.a:
• **Lung** (about 85% of cases), **oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus**
• **Stomach, pancreas, liver, colorectum**
• **Kidney and bladder**
• **Cervix**
• **Acute myeloid leukaemia**
cards.m: Smoke travels: mouth → lungs → blood → kidney → bladder. Cancer follows the path.

cards.q: How does smoking cause cardiovascular disease?
cards.a:
• **Endothelial dysfunction** and oxidative stress
• **Prothrombotic** state – platelet activation, raised fibrinogen
• Atherogenic lipids – **lower HDL**, oxidised LDL
• **Sympathetic stimulation** by nicotine – higher heart rate and BP, coronary vasoconstriction
• **Carbon monoxide** – reduced oxygen delivery
cards.m: Smoking makes blood sticky, vessels narrow and the heart work harder.

cards.q: Which vascular disease classically affects young male heavy smokers and how is it managed?
cards.a:
• **Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease)**
• Inflammatory occlusion of small/medium arteries of hands and feet → claudication, rest pain, digital ulcers, gangrene
• Typically young (<45) male smokers without other atherosclerotic risk factors
• **Complete smoking cessation** is the only treatment that halts progression; continued smoking → amputation
cards.m: Buerger's: 'Butt' (cigarette) → amputation if it goes on.

cards.q: What is the most important cause of COPD, and which intervention best slows lung function decline?
cards.a:
• **Cigarette smoking** is the main cause of COPD
• **Smoking cessation** is the intervention proven to slow the accelerated decline in **FEV1**
• Inhalers relieve symptoms and exacerbations but do not change the smoking-driven decline
cards.m: Fletcher–Peto curve: stop smoking and the FEV1 slope returns towards normal.

cards.q: What are the complications of smoking in pregnancy?
cards.a:
• **Miscarriage**, ectopic pregnancy
• **Placental abruption**, placenta praevia, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes
• **Fetal growth restriction / low birth weight**, **preterm birth**, stillbirth
• **Sudden infant death syndrome** after birth
• Orofacial clefts
cards.m: Smoking in pregnancy hits the placenta, the growth and the cot.

cards.q: How does smoking affect eligibility for the combined oral contraceptive pill (UKMEC)?
cards.a:
• Age **≥35 and ≥15 cigarettes/day** → **UKMEC 4** (unacceptable risk)
• Age ≥35 and <15/day, or stopped <1 year ago → **UKMEC 3**
• Age <35 smoker → UKMEC 2
• Offer progestogen-only methods or LARC instead
cards.m: 35 and 15 = COC is 4-bidden.

cards.q: List non-cancer, non-cardiorespiratory conditions caused or worsened by smoking.
cards.a:
• **Peptic ulcer** (delayed healing), **Crohn's disease** (worse course)
• **Osteoporosis** and hip fracture
• **Cataract** and **age-related macular degeneration**
• **Periodontal disease**, tooth loss
• **Erectile dysfunction**, reduced fertility
• **Type 2 diabetes**, psoriasis, Graves' ophthalmopathy, poor wound healing
cards.m: Bones, eyes, gums, gut, bedroom – all suffer.

cards.q: Smoking worsens Crohn's disease – which inflammatory bowel disease is the notable exception?
cards.a:
• **Ulcerative colitis** – smokers have lower risk, and some patients flare after quitting
• This is **never** a reason to start or continue smoking – the overall harms vastly outweigh it
• Crohn's disease: smoking increases risk, relapse and surgery
cards.m: Crohn's loves Cigarettes; UC is Un-Cigaretted (but never prescribe smoking).

cards.q: Why is smoking relevant to tuberculosis control in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Smoking increases the risk of **TB infection, active TB, and death from TB**
• Smokers have more relapse and poorer treatment outcomes
• Every TB patient who smokes should receive cessation support during treatment
cards.m: Smoke damages the lung's cleaners (cilia, macrophages) – TB walks in.

cards.q: How does smoking affect diabetes?
cards.a:
• Increases the risk of developing **type 2 diabetes** (about 30–40% higher)
• Worsens **insulin resistance** and glycaemic control
• Accelerates **macrovascular** (MI, stroke, PAD) and **microvascular** (nephropathy, retinopathy) complications
• Smoking cessation is part of every diabetic review
cards.m: Diabetes + smoking = double hit on the arteries.

cards.q: When should a smoker stop before elective surgery, and why?
cards.a:
• Ideally **at least 4 weeks (preferably 6–8) before** surgery
• Reduces **wound infection**, wound dehiscence, pulmonary and cardiac complications
• Any period of abstinence helps – CO clears within a day
• Stay smoke-free throughout recovery
cards.m: Four weeks smoke-free = healthier wounds and lungs on the operating table.

cards.q: What happens within 20 minutes and within 12 hours of stopping smoking (WHO timeline)?
cards.a:
• **20 minutes** – heart rate and blood pressure drop
• **12 hours** – carbon monoxide level in the blood drops to **normal**
cards.m: 20 minutes for the heart, 12 hours for the CO.

cards.q: What benefits occur at 2–12 weeks and 1–9 months after quitting (WHO timeline)?
cards.a:
• **2–12 weeks** – circulation improves and **lung function increases**
• **1–9 months** – **coughing and shortness of breath decrease**
cards.m: Weeks for circulation, months for cough.

cards.q: How is the risk of coronary heart disease reduced at 1 year and 15 years after quitting?
cards.a:
• **1 year** – CHD risk is about **half** that of a continuing smoker
• **15 years** – CHD risk is the **same as a non-smoker**
cards.m: 1 year: half the heart risk; 15 years: heart like a non-smoker.

cards.q: How do stroke and lung cancer risks fall after quitting (WHO timeline)?
cards.a:
• **Stroke** – reduced to that of a non-smoker **5–15 years** after quitting
• **Lung cancer** – at **10 years**, risk falls to about **half** that of a smoker
• Risks of mouth, throat, oesophagus, bladder, cervix and pancreas cancers also decrease
cards.m: 5 for stroke, 10 for lung, 15 for heart.

cards.q: How much life expectancy does smoking cost, and does quitting late still help?
cards.a:
• Lifelong smokers lose about **10 years** of life
• Quitting **before about 40** avoids around **90%** of the excess risk of death
• Quitting at **any age** gains life-years – even at 60, about 3 years
cards.m: It is never too late, but earlier is better.

cards.q: Is quitting worthwhile after a myocardial infarction?
cards.a:
• Yes – quitting after coronary heart disease reduces **all-cause mortality by about one-third**
• Benefit is comparable to or greater than many secondary-prevention drugs
• Cessation support is a core part of cardiac rehabilitation
cards.m: After an MI, stopping smoking works like an extra life-saving drug.

cards.q: What are the harms of second-hand smoke in children?
cards.a:
• **Sudden infant death syndrome**
• **Asthma** onset and exacerbations
• **Otitis media** (glue ear)
• **Lower respiratory tract infections** (bronchiolitis, pneumonia)
• Advise a completely **smoke-free home and car**
cards.m: SALO: SIDS, Asthma, LRTI, Otitis media.

cards.q: How much does smoking increase the risk of lung cancer?
cards.a:
• Smokers have about **15–30 times** the lung cancer risk of never-smokers
• About **85%** of lung cancers are caused by smoking
• Risk rises with **pack-years** and falls progressively after quitting

cards.q: Describe the chemistry of nicotine.
cards.a:
• **Natural liquid alkaloid** from *Nicotiana tabacum*
• **Colourless, volatile base**, **pKa 8.0**
• Structure: a **pyridine ring** joined to a **pyrrolidine ring**
cards.m: Nicotine is a base – bases love alkaline places.

cards.q: Why is nicotine absorption pH-dependent?
cards.a:
• Nicotine is a **weak base (pKa 8.0)**
• In **alkaline** media it is mainly **un-ionised** → crosses membranes → **well absorbed**
• In **acidic** media it is **ionised** → poorly absorbed
cards.m: Alkaline = absorbed; Acidic = Avoided.

cards.q: Why do cigar, pipe and spit-tobacco users absorb nicotine through the mouth, while cigarette smokers mostly do not?
cards.a:
• Mouth pH is about **7.0**
• **Cigarette smoke is acidic** → nicotine ionised → **limited buccal absorption** → cigarette smokers must inhale to absorb nicotine in the lungs
• **Pipes, cigars, spit tobacco and oral nicotine products are alkaline** → **significant buccal absorption**
cards.m: Cigarettes need the lungs; cigars can do it in the cheek.

cards.q: Through which routes is nicotine absorbed?
cards.a:
• **Respiratory epithelium** – rapid (smoking)
• **Intact skin** – basis of the **nicotine patch**
• **Buccal mucosa** – gum, lozenge, inhaler, spray
• **Small intestine** – swallowed nicotine (but large first-pass metabolism)
• Note: slide p12 lists these routes under 'Distribution'; they describe **absorption**
cards.m: Lungs, skin, cheek, gut – every NRT form uses one of these doors.

cards.q: What is the pH inside the mouth and how can beverages affect nicotine absorption?
cards.a:
• Mouth pH is about **7.0**
• Drinks change oral pH and therefore absorption
• **Acidic drinks** (coffee, cola, fruit juice) lower pH → nicotine ionised → **less buccal absorption** from gum, lozenge or inhaler
cards.m: Coffee and cola make the cheek acidic – nicotine bounces off.

cards.q: How quickly does inhaled nicotine reach the brain, and why does this speed matter?
cards.a:
• About **11 seconds** after inhalation – faster than an IV injection
• **Arterial** levels peak far higher than **venous** levels
• A rapid, high bolus gives an immediate reward linked to each puff → **strong reinforcement and addiction**
• NRT delivers nicotine slowly and at lower peaks, so it is far less addictive
cards.m: Puff to brain in 11 seconds – the fastest drug delivery system on the market.

cards.q: How is nicotine metabolised and excreted?
cards.a:
• Metabolised in the liver, mainly by **CYP2A6**
• **70–80%** converted to **cotinine**; other metabolites about 10%
• Excreted in **urine** and in **breast milk**
cards.m: Nicotine → Cotinine (C for 'converted').

cards.q: Compare the half-lives of nicotine and cotinine. Which is used as a biomarker of tobacco exposure?
cards.a:
• Nicotine half-life about **2 hours**
• Cotinine half-life about **16–20 hours**
• **Cotinine** (saliva, urine, serum) is the preferred biomarker of nicotine intake over the previous few days
• Limitation: cotinine is also positive in people using **NRT** or e-cigarettes
cards.m: Nicotine is a sprinter (2 h); cotinine is a marathon runner (~16–20 h).

cards.q: Why does nicotine excretion in breast milk matter clinically?
cards.a:
• Nicotine passes into **breast milk** → infant exposure
• Breastfeeding mothers should be supported to quit
• If NRT is needed, use **short-acting** forms **immediately after** a feed to minimise levels at the next feed
• Breastfeeding should still be encouraged
cards.m: Feed first, then NRT.

cards.q: Where in the body does nicotine act, and what is its overall effect?
cards.a:
• **Central** and **peripheral nervous systems**
• **Cardiovascular system**, **adrenal medulla** (catecholamine release)
• **Exocrine glands**, **gastrointestinal system**
• **Neuromuscular junction**, sensory receptors
• Overall: **predominantly stimulant** effects

cards.q: Which receptor and pathway mediate nicotine addiction?
cards.a:
• Nicotine binds **α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors** in the **ventral tegmental area**
• Triggers **dopamine release** in the **nucleus accumbens** (mesolimbic reward pathway)
• Same pathway targeted by **varenicline** (α4β2 partial agonist)
cards.m: α4β2 → VTA → dopamine in the nucleus accumbens = the reward circuit.

cards.q: Describe the cycle of nicotine addiction.
cards.a:
• Nicotine stimulates **dopamine release** → **pleasurable feelings**
• Leads to **repeat administration**
• **Tolerance** develops (more needed for the same effect)
• **Discontinuation → withdrawal symptoms** → smoking again to relieve them
cards.m: Pleasure → repeat → tolerance → withdrawal → relapse: the nicotine loop.

cards.q: What are the central nervous system effects of nicotine?
cards.a:
• **Pleasure**
• **Arousal**
• **Anxiety relief**
• **Improved task performance** (concentration)
• These perceived benefits explain why smokers feel they 'need' a cigarette to cope
cards.m: PAAI: Pleasure, Arousal, Anxiety relief, Improved performance.

cards.q: What are the cardiovascular effects of nicotine?
cards.a:
• **↑ Heart rate**
• **↑ Cardiac output**
• **↑ Blood pressure**
• **Coronary vasoconstriction**
• Mediated by sympathetic stimulation and adrenal catecholamine release
cards.m: Nicotine revs the engine and narrows the fuel line.

cards.q: Which non-CNS, non-CVS effects of nicotine explain weight gain after quitting?
cards.a:
• Nicotine causes **appetite suppression** and **increased metabolic rate**
• It also causes **skeletal muscle relaxation**
• On quitting, appetite rises and metabolic rate falls → average gain of about **4–5 kg** in the first year
cards.m: Remove the appetite-suppressant and the metabolic booster → the scale goes up.

cards.q: Which seven neurotransmitters are released by nicotine?
cards.a:
• **Dopamine**
• **Norepinephrine**
• **Acetylcholine**
• **Glutamate**
• **Serotonin**
• **β-Endorphin**
• **GABA**
• Each mediates part of the 'benefit' smokers feel – and its loss on quitting
cards.m: Seven messengers: Dopamine, NE, ACh, Glutamate, Serotonin, β-Endorphin, GABA – 'Do Not Accept Gifts So Easily, Guys'.

cards.q: Which nicotine-released neurotransmitters reduce anxiety and tension, and which modulate mood?
cards.a:
• **β-Endorphin** and **GABA** – reduction of **anxiety and tension**
• **Serotonin** – **mood modulation** and appetite suppression
• Explains why smokers report smoking to 'calm down' and why mood dips during withdrawal
cards.m: GABA and endorphins = the calm-down pair.

cards.q: Match dopamine, norepinephrine, acetylcholine and glutamate to their effects after nicotine.
cards.a:
• **Dopamine** – pleasure, reward
• **Norepinephrine** – arousal, appetite suppression
• **Acetylcholine** – arousal, cognitive enhancement
• **Glutamate** – learning, memory enhancement
cards.m: Dopamine delights, Noradrenaline wakes, ACh thinks, Glutamate remembers.

cards.q: Is nicotine itself the main cause of smoking-related disease? Why does this matter for NRT?
cards.a:
• **No** – disease is caused mainly by **tar (carcinogens)**, **carbon monoxide** and other combustion products
• Nicotine causes **addiction** and modest haemodynamic effects
• Therefore medicinal nicotine (NRT) is **far safer than smoking**, even in cardiovascular disease
cards.m: Nicotine is the hook, not the bullet.

cards.q: Why is the first cigarette of the morning the most satisfying, and why does it reflect dependence?
cards.a:
• Overnight abstinence → nicotine falls → **nicotinic receptors recover sensitivity** and withdrawal begins
• The first cigarette relieves withdrawal and gives the strongest reward
• Smoking **soon after waking** therefore signals high dependence – the highest-scoring item on the **Fagerström test**
cards.m: The sooner the first cigarette, the stronger the chain.

cards.q: What is a brief intervention for smoking cessation and why should every clinician deliver it?
cards.a:
• A short, structured interaction (often **under 3–5 minutes**) during a routine consultation – **5A, 3A or ABC**
• Even **advice lasting less than 3 minutes** increases quit rates
• Because most smokers see a doctor yearly, brief intervention gives huge population impact
cards.m: Three minutes of advice can add ten years of life.

cards.q: What are the 5A of brief intervention?
cards.a:
• **Ask** – about tobacco use
• **Advise** – to quit
• **Assess** – willingness to quit
• **Assist** – in the quit attempt
• **Arrange** – follow-up
cards.m: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange – 'Ask Advice Before Assisting And Arranging'.

cards.q: What are the 3A, and when are they used instead of the 5A?
cards.a:
• **Ask**, **Advise**, **Assist** (the 'Assist' may be direct help or **referral** to a quit service)
• Used by busy clinicians or those without cessation expertise
• The 5A adds **Assess** willingness and **Arrange** follow-up
cards.m: 3A is the express lane: ask, advise, and get them help.

cards.q: In the 'Ask' step, what question is asked and what are the four possible answers?
cards.a:
• 'Are you smoking?'
• **1.** Smoker, **willing** to make a quit attempt
• **2.** Smoker, **not willing** to make a quit attempt
• **3.** **Ex-smoker**
• **4.** **Non-smoker**

cards.q: Why should smoking status be documented at every visit?
cards.a:
• Smoking status should be treated like a **vital sign**
• Documentation triggers advice at each contact and tracks progress
• Ex-smokers need reinforcement (relapse prevention); non-smokers need reinforcement and second-hand-smoke advice
cards.m: BP, pulse, temperature – and tobacco.

cards.q: How should the 'Advise' step be delivered? Give an example.
cards.a:
• **Clear, strong and personalised** advice
• Example: 'I think it is important for you to quit smoking now and I can help you'
• Or: 'As your clinician, I need you to know that quitting smoking is the most important thing you can do to protect your health now and in the future. The clinic staff and I will help you'
• Link to the patient's own illness where possible
cards.m: Clear, Strong, Personal – no 'cut down a bit'.

cards.q: What does the 'Assess' step determine and how does it direct the next action?
cards.a:
• Asks: 'Are you willing to quit smoking?'
• **Willing** → provide **assistance** (counselling, pharmacotherapy, STAR)
• **Unwilling** → provide **motivational intervention using the 5R**
cards.m: Willing → Assist; Unwilling → 5R.

cards.q: Which model describes how smokers move towards quitting, and what are its stages?
cards.a:
• **Stages of change (transtheoretical model) – Prochaska & DiClemente**
• **Precontemplation → Contemplation → Preparation → Action → Maintenance**, with **Relapse** possible at any stage
• Movement is a cycle, not a straight line
cards.m: Please Can Pete Act More Reliably.

cards.q: Describe the precontemplation stage.
cards.a:
• 'I am **not aware** my smoking is a problem. I have **no intention** to quit'
• Not intending to change in the **next 6 months**
• Approach: raise awareness with the **5R**; respect autonomy and repeat at each visit
cards.m: Pre-contemplation = pre-thinking: has not even thought about quitting.

cards.q: Describe the contemplation stage.
cards.a:
• 'I know my smoking is a problem. I want to stop but **no plan yet**'
• Intends to change within the next **6 months**; **ambivalent**
• Approach: **5R / motivational interviewing** to resolve ambivalence
cards.m: Contemplation = thinking about it, sitting on the fence.

cards.q: Describe the preparation stage and the matching intervention.
cards.a:
• 'I am **making plans** and changing things'
• Intends to quit within the **next 30 days**; may have taken small steps
• Approach: **set a quit date (STAR)**, offer **pharmacotherapy** and counselling
cards.m: Preparation = packing the bags; set the departure (quit) date.

cards.q: How are the action and maintenance stages distinguished?
cards.a:
• **Action** – 'I have stopped smoking'; quit within the past **6 months**
• **Maintenance** – 'I am continuing to not smoke. I sometimes miss it, but I am still not smoking'; abstinent for **more than 6 months**
• Both need follow-up and relapse-prevention support
cards.m: Under 6 months = Action; over 6 months = Maintenance.

cards.q: How should relapse be viewed and managed?
cards.a:
• 'I miss smoking so much that I need a cigarette again'
• A **normal part of the cycle** – many smokers make **several attempts** before stopping for good
• Avoid blame; review what triggered it, learn from it and re-enter **contemplation/preparation**
cards.m: Relapse is a lesson, not a failure.

cards.q: Match each stage of change to the most appropriate intervention.
cards.a:
• **Precontemplation / contemplation** → **5R** motivational intervention
• **Preparation** → set quit date (**STAR**), pharmacotherapy, counselling
• **Action** → close follow-up, manage withdrawal, adjust medication
• **Maintenance** → reinforce success, relapse prevention
• **Relapse** → non-judgemental review, re-plan
cards.m: Not ready → motivate; ready → assist; done → protect.

cards.q: What are the components of the 'Assist' step?
cards.a:
• **Counselling**
• **Pharmacotherapy**
• **STAR** method
• **Others** – supportive healthcare environment, explore past quit experience, limit/abstain from alcohol, provide supplementary materials

cards.q: What does the STAR method stand for?
cards.a:
• **S – Set** a quit date (**within 2 weeks**)
• **T – Tell** family, friends and co-workers about quitting
• **A – Anticipate** challenges, including withdrawal symptoms
• **R – Remove** tobacco products (home, car, workplace)
cards.m: STAR: Set, Tell, Anticipate, Remove.

cards.q: Why is the quit date set within 2 weeks?
cards.a:
• Close enough to **keep motivation high**
• Far enough to **prepare** – tell others, remove cigarettes, plan for triggers
• Allows **pre-loading** of varenicline or bupropion (started 1–2 weeks before the quit date)
cards.m: Within 2 weeks: before the motivation fades, after the medicine kicks in.

cards.q: Why ask about past quit attempts and alcohol use during 'Assist'?
cards.a:
• **Past quit experience** – what helped, what caused relapse (e.g. withdrawal, stress, social triggers) → tailor the plan
• **Alcohol** – a major relapse trigger; advise to **limit or abstain** during the quit attempt
• Also provide a **supportive healthcare environment** and **supplementary materials**
cards.m: Yesterday's relapse is today's roadmap.

cards.q: What is the recommended follow-up schedule after the quit date?
cards.a:
• **First week** after the quit date
• **Weekly** in the first month
• **Every 2 weeks** in the 2nd and 3rd months
• **Monthly** thereafter up to **6 months**
cards.m: 1 – weekly – fortnightly – monthly: the follow-up slows as the risk falls.

cards.q: Why is the first follow-up arranged within the first week after the quit date?
cards.a:
• **Withdrawal symptoms peak** in the first few days and **relapse risk is highest** early
• Early review allows dose adjustment, managing side effects and reinforcing motivation
cards.m: The first week is the danger week.

cards.q: What should be done at each follow-up visit?
cards.a:
• Can be **in person, by telephone or virtual**
• **Assess pharmacotherapy use** and problems (adherence, side effects)
• **Congratulate** if abstinent
• If tobacco use has occurred: **review the situation** and **assess commitment to total abstinence**

cards.q: A patient smoked a few cigarettes during the quit attempt. How do you manage this lapse?
cards.a:
• Do **not** label it a failure or stop treatment
• **Review the circumstances** (trigger, place, people, alcohol)
• **Reassess commitment** to total abstinence and recommit to 'not a single puff'
• **Continue pharmacotherapy**; check dose and technique
cards.m: A slip is not a fall – unless you stop the treatment.

cards.q: What does the ABC approach stand for?
cards.a:
• **A – Ask** about and document smoking status
• **B – Brief advice** to stop
• **C – Cessation support** – provide it, or **refer** to a smoking cessation service
• An alternative to 5A for busy settings
cards.m: ABC: Ask, Brief advice, Cessation support.

cards.q: What are the four elements of 'Brief advice' in the ABC approach?
cards.a:
• **Advise all** people who smoke
• **Personalise** the advice – link smoking to the current health problem and how stopping may help; highlight the benefits of quitting
• **Acknowledge** that many people make **several attempts** before stopping completely
• **Document** that advice was given
cards.m: All, Personal, Acknowledge, Document – 'APAD'.

cards.q: In the ABC approach, what is 'Cessation support' and who should refer rather than treat?
cards.a:
• **Provide support** if able: set a quit date, assess nicotine dependence, arrange medication and follow-up
• **Refer** to a smoking cessation service if the healthcare worker lacks the **expertise or time**
• Either way, every smoker leaves with a route to help
cards.m: C = Care yourself, or Connect to a quit service.

cards.q: What is the Fagerström Test for Nicotine Dependence (FTND) and why is it used?
cards.a:
• A **6-item** questionnaire scored **0–10**
• Measures the **degree of physical nicotine dependence**
• Guides the **intensity and dose of pharmacotherapy** and predicts withdrawal severity
cards.m: FTND tells you how tight the nicotine grip is.

cards.q: How is the FTND item 'How soon after waking do you smoke your first cigarette?' scored?
cards.a:
• **Within 5 minutes – 3 points**
• **5–30 minutes – 2 points**
• **31–60 minutes – 1 point**
• **After 60 minutes – 0 points**

cards.q: How is the FTND item 'How many cigarettes do you smoke each day?' scored?
cards.m: Each extra 10 sticks above 10 adds a point.

cards.q: Which four FTND items score 1 point for a 'yes' answer?
cards.a:
• **Difficult not to smoke** where forbidden (e.g. school, cinema, library, bus, hospital)
• The cigarette you would most hate to give up is **the first one in the morning**
• Smoke **more during the first few hours** after waking than the rest of the day
• Still smoke when **so ill you are in bed** most of the day
cards.m: Forbidden places, First of the morning, First few hours, Flat in bed – the four F's.

cards.q: How is the total FTND score interpreted (per the lecture)?
cards.a:
• Maximum score **10**
• **7–10 – highly dependent**
• **4–6 – moderately dependent**
• **<4 – minimally dependent**
cards.m: Seven and above = heavy grip; four to six = medium; under four = mild.

cards.q: Which two FTND items carry the most weight, and what short tool uses them?
cards.a:
• **Time to first cigarette** after waking and **cigarettes per day** (each scores up to 3)
• Together they form the **Heaviness of Smoking Index (HSI, 0–6)** – a quick screen in a busy clinic
• Time to first cigarette is the single best predictor of dependence
cards.m: When and how many – the two questions that matter most.

cards.q: Mr Ali (50, COPD) smokes 30 sticks/day, smokes right after waking and failed a 2-day cold-turkey attempt because of withdrawal. His FTND is 9/10. Interpret this.
cards.a:
• FTND **9 = highly dependent** (7–10)
• Explains early relapse with cold turkey: withdrawal overwhelmed him
• Needs **intensive behavioural support plus effective pharmacotherapy** (e.g. **varenicline** or **combination NRT**) to control withdrawal
cards.m: High score, high support – willpower alone failed for a reason.

cards.q: How is a carbon monoxide (CO) breath analyser used in smoking cessation?
cards.a:
• Measures **exhaled CO in ppm**; reflects smoking over roughly the past **day**
• Smokers usually read above about **10 ppm**; non-smokers usually below about **7 ppm** (cut-offs vary)
• **Motivates** patients (visible fall after quitting) and **verifies abstinence**
• Unaffected by NRT – unlike cotinine
• Recommended to record status in psychiatric patients together with FTND
cards.m: CO meter = a breathalyser for smoke.

cards.q: What happens physiologically when a smoker stops smoking?
cards.a:
• Body **nicotine level falls**
• The brain, adapted to nicotine (upregulated receptors, reduced dopamine tone without it), reacts → **withdrawal symptoms**
• Withdrawal is the commonest reason for early relapse

cards.q: List the symptoms of nicotine withdrawal.
cards.a:
• **Irritability**, frustration or anger
• **Anxiety** and **restlessness**
• **Difficulty concentrating**
• **Depressed mood**
• **Insomnia**
• **Increased appetite** / weight gain
• **Cravings** (urges to smoke)
cards.m: Withdrawal makes you 'MAD-HIC': Mood low, Anxiety, Difficulty concentrating, Hunger, Irritability, Cravings (+ insomnia).

cards.q: What is the time course of nicotine withdrawal?
cards.a:
• Begins within **hours** of the last cigarette
• **Peaks in the first few days** (first week)
• Most symptoms **subside over 2–4 weeks**
• This is why early follow-up (first week) is crucial
cards.m: Hours to start, days to peak, weeks to fade.

cards.q: How long does a single strong urge to smoke typically last?
cards.a:
• Usually only about **3 minutes**
• Teach patients to **ride it out** with the **4D** (deep breathing, drink water, divert thinking, discuss with a friend)
• Each urge resisted weakens the next
cards.m: The urge is a wave – it peaks and passes in about 3 minutes.

cards.q: Which withdrawal-related features persist longest after quitting?
cards.a:
• **Increased appetite** – may last **10 weeks or more**
• **Cravings** – can persist for **months**, often **cue-triggered** (coffee, meals, alcohol, stress, smoking friends)
• Other symptoms (irritability, poor concentration, insomnia) usually settle in **2–4 weeks**
cards.m: Hunger and cravings are the last guests to leave the party.

cards.q: A patient's cough worsens 1–2 weeks after quitting. What is the likely explanation?
cards.a:
• Recovery of **mucociliary clearance** – cilia start clearing accumulated mucus
• Usually **temporary** and settles within weeks
• Reassure, but evaluate if red flags (haemoptysis, weight loss, fever, persistent cough beyond several weeks)
cards.m: The cough after quitting is the lungs spring-cleaning.

cards.q: Why do withdrawal symptoms matter when planning a quit attempt?
cards.a:
• They are the **most common cause of early relapse** (e.g. Mr Ali relapsed after 2 days of cold turkey)
• **Anticipate** them (STAR) and treat with **pharmacotherapy** plus coping strategies
• Fear of withdrawal is itself a **roadblock** that stops people trying
cards.m: Treat the withdrawal and you protect the quit.

cards.q: Why might a recent quitter who drinks a lot of coffee develop jitteriness and palpitations?
cards.a:
• Tobacco smoke (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons) **induces CYP1A2**, which metabolises **caffeine**
• After quitting, induction wears off → **caffeine levels can roughly double**
• Symptoms mimic withdrawal (anxiety, insomnia, palpitations)
• Advise **halving caffeine intake** during the quit attempt
cards.m: Same coffee, half the clearance – cut the cups.

cards.q: Which smokers should receive the 5R motivational intervention?
cards.a:
• Smokers who are **unwilling to quit** at present (precontemplation and contemplation)
• Identified at the **Assess** step of the 5A
• Aim: **enhance motivation** to make a future quit attempt
cards.m: 5R is for the 'not now' smoker.

cards.q: What are the 5R?
cards.a:
• **Relevance**
• **Risks**
• **Rewards**
• **Roadblocks**
• **Repetition**
cards.m: Real Reasons Reward Removing Roadblocks Repeatedly.

cards.q: What does 'Relevance' involve in the 5R?
cards.a:
• Encourage the patient to say **why quitting is personally relevant**, as **specifically** as possible
• E.g. own disease (asthma, diabetes, angina), family situation, children, age, past quit experience
cards.m: Relevance = 'Why does this matter to YOU?'

cards.q: What does 'Risks' involve in the 5R? Give examples.
cards.a:
• Ask the patient to **identify negative consequences** of tobacco use
• **Acute** – breathlessness, asthma exacerbations, erectile dysfunction, infertility, raised CO
• **Long-term** – MI, stroke, cancers, COPD
• **Environmental** – second-hand smoke harming spouse and children
cards.m: Risks = what smoking takes away.

cards.q: What does 'Rewards' involve in the 5R? Give examples.
cards.a:
• Ask the patient to **identify potential benefits of stopping**
• Better health, improved **taste and smell**, **saving money**, better breathing and fitness
• Healthier children and babies, being a good role model, fresher breath and home, feeling in control
cards.m: Rewards = what quitting gives back.

cards.q: What does 'Roadblocks' involve in the 5R?
cards.a:
• Ask the patient to **identify barriers** to quitting
• Then provide **treatment or solutions that address those barriers** (e.g. pharmacotherapy for withdrawal, dietary advice for weight concerns)
cards.m: Roadblocks: name the obstacle, then clear it.

cards.q: What does 'Repetition' involve in the 5R?
cards.a:
• The motivational intervention is **repeated every time** an unmotivated patient visits the clinic
• Most smokers need **multiple contacts and attempts** before quitting
• Document each discussion
cards.m: Repetition: drip, drip, drip – the stone eventually wears.

cards.q: List common roadblocks to quitting.
cards.a:
• **Withdrawal symptoms**
• **Fear of failure**
• **Weight gain**
• **Lack of support**
• **Depression**
• **Enjoyment of tobacco**
• **Being around tobacco users**
• **Limited knowledge** of effective treatment options
cards.m: 'WFW LDE BL' – Withdrawal, Failure, Weight, Lack of support, Depression, Enjoyment, Being around smokers, Limited knowledge.

cards.q: How can the roadblocks of withdrawal, weight gain and depression be addressed?
cards.a:
• **Withdrawal** → effective **pharmacotherapy** (NRT, varenicline, bupropion) and coping skills
• **Weight gain** → explain average gain (about 4–5 kg) is far less harmful than smoking; diet and exercise; NRT/bupropion can **delay** gain
• **Depression** → screen and treat; bupropion or nortriptyline may help both
cards.m: Match each barrier to a specific fix.

cards.q: How do you address 'fear of failure' as a roadblock?
cards.a:
• Normalise: most ex-smokers needed **several attempts** before succeeding
• Each attempt teaches what triggers relapse
• Using **pharmacotherapy plus behavioural support** greatly improves the odds compared with willpower alone
cards.m: Every failed attempt is a rehearsal for the successful one.

cards.q: How do you address 'enjoyment of tobacco' and 'being around tobacco users' as roadblocks?
cards.a:
• Identify the **situations and people** linked with smoking
• Change routines (e.g. leave the table after meals), avoid smoking areas early on
• Ask family and colleagues not to smoke around or offer cigarettes; make home and car **smoke-free**
• Replace the 'reward' with alternatives (exercise, hobbies, saved money)
cards.m: Change the scene and the script changes.

cards.q: How does 'limited knowledge of effective treatment options' act as a roadblock, and how is it overcome?
cards.a:
• Many smokers believe quitting relies on **willpower alone** (cold turkey), which has low success
• Explain that **pharmacotherapy roughly doubles** quit rates and **combining it with behavioural support** improves them further
• Tell them about free help at **Klinik Kesihatan quit clinics** and **mQuit** services
cards.m: They are not weak – they were just unarmed.

cards.q: What are the core principles of motivational interviewing used with unwilling smokers?
cards.a:
• **Express empathy** – reflective listening, no lecturing
• **Develop discrepancy** – between smoking and the patient's own goals
• **Roll with resistance** – avoid arguing
• **Support self-efficacy** – belief that change is possible
• Skills: **OARS** – Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries
cards.m: Guide, don't drag.

cards.q: Which services provide smoking cessation help in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Klinik Kesihatan** (quit smoking clinics)
• **Hospitals**
• **mQuit services** – a smoking cessation programme involving the **public and private sectors**

cards.q: What is mQuit and why is it useful for patients?
cards.a:
• MOH smoking cessation programme linking **public and private** providers (e.g. government clinics, hospitals, private GP clinics, community pharmacies)
• Gives smokers more **access points** near home or work
• Useful referral route when the treating clinician lacks time or expertise
cards.m: mQuit = many doors to quitting.

cards.q: What are the two arms of smoking cessation treatment?
cards.a:
• **Non-pharmacological** – behavioural intervention
• **Pharmacological** – **nicotine-based** (NRT) and **non-nicotine-based** (varenicline, bupropion, nortriptyline)

cards.q: Which smokers attempting to quit should be offered pharmacotherapy?
cards.a:
• **All** smokers attempting to quit, **unless contraindicated**
• Pharmacotherapy is not reserved for heavy smokers – dose is adjusted to dependence
cards.m: Every quit attempt deserves medication unless there's a reason not to.

cards.q: What is the most effective overall strategy for quitting?
cards.a:
• **Combining behavioural intervention with medication** increases the chance of quitting more than either alone
• Medication blunts withdrawal; behavioural support handles habits, triggers and motivation
cards.m: Pills for the chemistry, counselling for the habit.

cards.q: In what formats can behavioural support be delivered?
cards.a:
• **Individual** face-to-face counselling
• **Group** sessions
• **Telephone** counselling / quitlines
• **Text messaging**, apps and websites
• **Self-help materials**
• More sessions and more contact time give higher quit rates (dose–response)
cards.m: More contact, more quitters.

cards.q: What are the 4D for overcoming a strong urge to smoke?
cards.a:
• **Deep breathing**
• **Drink plenty of water**
• **Divert your thinking** (do something else)
• **Discuss with a friend**
• The urge typically passes in about **3 minutes**
cards.m: 4D: Deep breathe, Drink, Divert, Discuss.

cards.q: Give practical examples of 'Divert your thinking' during an urge.
cards.a:
• **Wash face and hands**
• **5 minutes of exercise**
• **Cold bath**
• **Munch something** (preferably healthy)
• **Keep hands busy**
cards.m: Busy hands, busy mind, no cigarette.

cards.q: How does exercise help a person who is quitting?
cards.a:
• Even **short bouts** (about 5 minutes) reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms
• Improves mood and stress
• Helps limit **post-cessation weight gain**
cards.m: Move when the urge comes.

cards.q: How do you help a smoker identify and manage triggers (e.g. Mr Ali smokes after meals, when bored or stressed, and with colleagues)?
cards.a:
• Ask the patient to list **when, where and with whom** they smoke (a smoking diary helps)
• Plan a **specific alternative** for each trigger: leave the table/brush teeth after meals, a hobby for boredom, breathing or a walk for stress, avoid smoking breaks with colleagues
• Use short-acting NRT for predictable high-risk moments
cards.m: Know the trigger, prepare the swap.

cards.q: Why advise a smoke-free home and car, and what does Malaysian law say about smoke-free places?
cards.a:
• Removes cues, protects family from **second-hand smoke**, supports abstinence
• Smoking is banned at **all eating premises** in Malaysia (from **2019**)
• The **Control of Smoking Products for Public Health Act 2024 (Act 852)** regulates tobacco **and vape** products, including a ban on sale to under-18s
cards.m: Smoke-free spaces make smoke-free people.

cards.q: Abrupt cessation or gradual reduction – which approach is recommended?
cards.a:
• **Abrupt cessation** on a quit date gives slightly higher success
• **Gradual reduction** ('cut down to quit', often with NRT) is acceptable for those unwilling to stop abruptly
• Unassisted 'cold turkey' with willpower alone succeeds in only about **3–5%** at one year – offer support and medication
cards.m: Stopping on a date beats drifting down – but any route with help beats none.

cards.q: What relapse-prevention skills should a quitter be taught?
cards.a:
• Recognise **high-risk situations**: alcohol, stress, social gatherings with smokers, meals and coffee
• Have a **coping plan** for each (4D, short-acting NRT, leave the situation)
• Adopt a **'not a single puff'** rule – one cigarette often leads to full relapse
• Seek help early after any lapse
cards.m: One puff opens the door – keep it shut.

cards.q: List the pharmacological options for smoking cessation.
cards.a:
• **Nicotine-based (NRT)** – gum, patch, spray, inhaler, lozenges
• **Non-nicotine-based** – **varenicline**, **bupropion SR**, **nortriptyline**
cards.m: Five nicotine forms, three non-nicotine pills.

cards.q: What four factors guide the choice of first-line pharmacotherapy?
cards.a:
• **Efficacy**
• **Safety**
• **Suitability** (patient preference, comorbidities, contraindications, previous experience)
• **Cost**
cards.m: ESSC: Efficacy, Safety, Suitability, Cost.

cards.q: How does nicotine replacement therapy work?
cards.a:
• Delivers nicotine to **replace the nicotine obtained from cigarettes**
• **Reduces withdrawal symptoms** and cravings
• Without the tar, CO and other toxins of smoke
cards.m: NRT keeps the nicotine, cuts the poison.

cards.q: How long is NRT used?
cards.a:
• **8–12 weeks**
• **Longer if needed** to prevent relapse
• Dose is usually tapered towards the end

cards.q: How does the level of dependence affect NRT dosing?
cards.a:
• **Heavier smokers usually need higher doses**
• Use **FTND / time to first cigarette / cigarettes per day** to choose strength (e.g. 21 mg patch, 4 mg gum)
• Under-dosing is a common reason for NRT failure
cards.m: Dose to the dependence, not to the fear.

cards.q: Can NRT be used by smokers who are not yet ready to stop completely?
cards.a:
• **Yes** – NRT can be used to **reduce cigarette intake before stopping** ('cut down to quit')
• Aim to set a quit date as the patient's confidence grows
• Smoking while using NRT is not dangerous

cards.q: What is the legal status of NRT products in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **Group C poisons** under the **Poisons Act 1952**
• Group C items can be supplied by a **registered pharmacist** without a doctor's prescription (as well as by doctors)
• Makes NRT accessible through community pharmacies
cards.m: Group C = Chemist can supply.

cards.q: Why is NRT far less addictive than smoking?
cards.a:
• Cigarettes deliver a **rapid, high arterial bolus** reaching the brain in about **11 seconds**
• NRT gives **slower absorption and lower peak levels** → much weaker reinforcement
• Long-term NRT dependence is uncommon and far safer than smoking
cards.m: Speed is what makes a drug addictive – NRT drives slowly.

cards.q: Compare long-acting and short-acting NRT.
cards.a:
• **Long-acting – patch**: steady background nicotine level; easy adherence; cannot be adjusted for sudden cravings
• **Short-acting – gum, lozenge, inhaler, spray**: patient-controlled doses for **breakthrough cravings** and trigger situations
• Short-acting forms need correct technique and frequent dosing
cards.m: Patch = baseline; short-acting = rescue.

cards.q: What is the most effective way to use NRT?
cards.a:
• **Combination NRT** – **patch plus a short-acting form** (gum, lozenge, inhaler or spray)
• More effective than any single NRT form
• Efficacy similar to **varenicline**
• Particularly for **highly dependent** smokers
cards.m: Two NRTs are better than one.

cards.q: What are the common nicotine patch strengths and how is the starting dose chosen?
cards.a:
• **24-hour patch**: 21 mg, 14 mg, 7 mg
• **16-hour patch**: 25 mg, 15 mg, 10 mg
• **>10 cigarettes/day** → start **21 mg/24 h** (or 25 mg/16 h)
• **≤10 cigarettes/day** → start **14 mg/24 h** (or 15 mg/16 h)
• Step down over 8–12 weeks
cards.m: Ten is the dividing line: more than 10 sticks → the highest patch.

cards.q: How should a nicotine patch be applied?
cards.a:
• Apply each morning to **clean, dry, hairless skin** (upper arm, chest, back, hip)
• Press firmly for about **10 seconds**
• **Rotate sites** daily; avoid the same site for several days
• Start on the **quit date**; can shower with it on
cards.m: New day, new patch, new place.

cards.q: How do 16-hour and 24-hour patches differ, and when is each preferred?
cards.a:
• **24-hour**: covers **morning cravings** on waking
• **16-hour** (worn while awake, removed at bedtime): fewer **sleep disturbances / vivid dreams**
• If a 24-hour patch causes vivid dreams or insomnia, **remove it at bedtime**
cards.m: Bad dreams? Take the patch off at bedtime.

cards.q: What are the common adverse effects of the nicotine patch and how are they managed?
cards.a:
• **Local skin irritation** (redness, itch) – rotate sites; topical hydrocortisone; change brand if persistent
• **Sleep disturbance / vivid dreams** – remove at bedtime
• Generalised rash is rare – stop if it occurs

cards.q: How is the strength of nicotine gum chosen?
cards.a:
• **4 mg** for highly dependent smokers – e.g. first cigarette **within 30 minutes** of waking (or about 20–25 or more cigarettes/day)
• **2 mg** for less dependent smokers
cards.m: Smokes within 30 minutes → 4 mg.

cards.q: Describe the 'chew and park' technique for nicotine gum.
cards.a:
• **Chew slowly** until a **peppery taste or tingling** appears
• **Park** the gum between cheek and gum until the tingle fades (about a minute)
• Repeat chew-and-park for about **30 minutes**, then discard
• Nicotine is absorbed through the **buccal mucosa**, not swallowed
cards.m: Chew – tingle – park – repeat.

cards.q: How often should nicotine gum be used?
cards.a:
• Regular use: **1 piece every 1–2 hours** initially (at least about 9 pieces a day)
• Plus extra pieces for cravings; maximum about **24 pieces a day**
• Reduce gradually over about **12 weeks**
• Using too little, too late is a common reason for failure
cards.m: By the clock, not only by the craving.

cards.q: A patient chews nicotine gum like ordinary gum and gets hiccups, heartburn and nausea. Why?
cards.a:
• Vigorous chewing releases nicotine too fast → it is **swallowed** rather than absorbed buccally
• Swallowed nicotine causes **hiccups, dyspepsia, nausea** and is less effective (first-pass metabolism)
• Re-teach **chew-and-park**
• Gum also causes jaw ache and is unsuitable with **dentures** or TMJ problems – consider a lozenge
cards.m: Chewing gum is not chewing gum – park it.

cards.q: What drink advice should be given with nicotine gum or lozenges?
cards.a:
• Avoid **acidic drinks** (coffee, cola, fruit juice, carbonated drinks) **for 15 minutes before and during** use
• They lower oral pH → nicotine becomes ionised → **less buccal absorption**
• Also avoid eating while using
cards.m: No coffee with your gum.

cards.q: How should nicotine lozenges be used?
cards.a:
• **Suck slowly** and move from side to side until dissolved (about 20–30 minutes)
• **Do not chew or swallow** whole
• **4 mg** if first cigarette within 30 minutes of waking; otherwise **2 mg**
• Suitable for people who cannot use gum (dentures, jaw problems)
cards.m: Lozenge: let it melt, don't bite.

cards.q: What is the nicotine inhaler and which smoker does it suit?
cards.a:
• A plastic mouthpiece holding a **nicotine cartridge**; puffing delivers nicotine absorbed in the **mouth and throat**, not the lungs
• Suits smokers who miss the **hand-to-mouth ritual**
• Needs frequent puffing; side effects: **throat irritation, cough**
cards.m: Inhaler: the ritual without the smoke.

cards.q: What are the features of nicotine spray (nasal or oral)?
cards.a:
• **Fastest-acting** NRT – useful for sudden strong cravings and highly dependent smokers
• Side effects: **nasal/throat irritation, sneezing, watery eyes, cough**
• Usually combined with a patch
cards.m: Spray = the fastest rescue.

cards.q: Is NRT safe in cardiovascular disease?
cards.a:
• Safe in **stable cardiovascular disease** – far safer than continued smoking (no CO or tar)
• **Caution** in the acute phase: **MI within about 2 weeks**, **unstable/worsening angina**, **serious arrhythmias**, recent stroke
• In these, prioritise behavioural support and use NRT **under medical supervision**
cards.m: Stable heart: NRT is fine. Fresh MI: go carefully, but smoking is still worse.

cards.q: What are the signs of nicotine excess from NRT?
cards.a:
• **Nausea, vomiting**, abdominal pain
• **Dizziness, headache**
• **Palpitations**, cold sweat, weakness
• Common cause: **continuing to smoke heavily** on high-dose NRT
• Action: stop smoking, **reduce the NRT dose**
cards.m: Too much nicotine feels like the first cigarette ever – sick and dizzy.

cards.q: A patient on NRT smokes a cigarette. Is it dangerous, and what should you advise?
cards.a:
• **Not dangerous** – the old myth that smoking on NRT causes a heart attack is unfounded
• Encourage **continuing NRT** and recommitting to abstinence
• Check dose is adequate and review the trigger

cards.q: What is a reasonable treatment plan for Mr Ali (30 sticks/day, FTND 9, COPD, failed cold turkey due to withdrawal, worried and confused)?
cards.a:
• Address worries: explain withdrawal and that medication controls it
• **Pharmacotherapy**: **varenicline** or **combination NRT** (21 mg patch + 4 mg gum/lozenge for cravings)
• **Behavioural support**: STAR, trigger plan (meals, boredom, stress, colleagues), 4D
• **Follow-up**: first week, then weekly in month 1
• Optimise COPD care
cards.m: High dependence + previous withdrawal failure = strongest medication + support.

cards.q: How does varenicline work?
cards.a:
• A selective **α4β2 nicotinic receptor partial agonist**
• **Agonist** action → maintains a **moderate dopamine level** → relieves **withdrawal** and cravings
• **Antagonist** action → blocks nicotine binding → **reduces smoking satisfaction**
cards.m: Varenicline: half key in the lock – opens a little, blocks the real key.

cards.q: How effective is varenicline compared with NRT?
cards.a:
• About **50% more effective** than any **single-form NRT**
• **Similar efficacy** to **combination NRT** (two NRTs)
cards.m: Varenicline ≈ two NRTs > one NRT.

cards.q: What is the standard varenicline dosing schedule?
cards.a:
• **Days 1–3: 0.5 mg once daily**
• **Days 4–7: 0.5 mg twice daily**
• **Day 8 onwards: 1 mg twice daily**
• Total course **12 weeks**
cards.m: 3 days half-once, 4 days half-twice, then one-twice.

cards.q: When is varenicline started relative to the quit date, and how long is it continued?
cards.a:
• Start **1–2 weeks before the quit date** (quit usually between **day 8 and day 14**)
• Continue for **12 weeks**
• A further **12 weeks** may be given to those who have quit, to reduce relapse
cards.m: Start first, quit second.

cards.q: What should a patient be told when starting varenicline?
cards.a:
• Keep smoking normally during the first week while the dose builds up
• Cigarettes may become **less satisfying** – this is the drug working
• Stop completely on the quit date (day 8–14); a flexible quit date up to about day 35 is also acceptable
• Take **after food with a full glass of water**
cards.m: Week one: smoke and titrate. Quit day: stop.

cards.q: What are the common adverse effects of varenicline?
cards.a:
• **Nausea** – the **commonest** (about 3 in 10); reduce by taking **after food with water**
• **Abnormal / vivid dreams**
• **Sleep disturbance** (insomnia)
• Also headache
cards.m: Varenicline = Vomit-y, Vivid dreams.

cards.q: What serious adverse effects are listed for varenicline, and what should a patient do if mood changes?
cards.a:
• **Cardiovascular events**, **depression**, **suicidal ideation**, **suicide**
• If mood or behaviour changes → **stop varenicline and contact a healthcare provider immediately**
• Note: the large EAGLES trial (2016) did not show a significant excess of neuropsychiatric events, but monitoring is still advised

cards.q: Who cannot use varenicline?
cards.a:
• **Pregnant** or **breastfeeding** women
• **Adolescents under 18 years**
• Use with caution / reduced dose in severe renal impairment
cards.m: Not for the bump, the breast or the young.

cards.q: How is varenicline adjusted in renal impairment, and why does it have few drug interactions?
cards.a:
• Excreted **largely unchanged by the kidneys** – minimal hepatic metabolism → **few drug interactions**
• Severe renal impairment (**CrCl <30 mL/min**): start **0.5 mg once daily**, maximum **0.5 mg twice daily**
• End-stage renal disease on dialysis: maximum 0.5 mg once daily
cards.m: Kidney clears it, so kidneys set the dose.

cards.q: What is bupropion and how does it help smokers quit?
cards.a:
• An **atypical antidepressant** – inhibits **dopamine and noradrenaline reuptake**; also a nicotinic receptor antagonist
• **Reduces the severity of tobacco withdrawal**
• Approximately **doubles** the chance of stopping smoking
cards.m: Bupropion boosts dopamine without nicotine.

cards.q: When is bupropion started and how long is it used?
cards.a:
• Start **at least 1 week before the quit date** (usually 1–2 weeks)
• Use for **at least 7 weeks** (typically 7–12 weeks)
• Needs time to reach steady state before the quit date
cards.m: Bupropion: one week before, seven weeks after.

cards.q: What is the usual dose of bupropion SR for smoking cessation?
cards.a:
• **150 mg once daily** for the first few days (3 days in most regimens; 6 days in the UK label)
• Then **150 mg twice daily**, doses **at least 8 hours apart**
• **Maximum 300 mg/day**; 150 mg daily only in hepatic/renal impairment or seizure risk factors
cards.m: 150 then 150 × 2 – never more than 300.

cards.q: What are the common adverse effects of bupropion and how is insomnia minimised?
cards.a:
• **Dry mouth**, **insomnia**, **headache**
• Also nausea, tremor, rash, raised blood pressure
• Insomnia: give the second dose in the **afternoon** (at least 8 h after the first) rather than at bedtime
cards.m: Bupropion keeps you up: Dry, Awake, Headachy.

cards.q: What are the contraindications to bupropion?
cards.a:
• **Seizure disorder** or history of seizures; **CNS tumour**
• **Eating disorders** (bulimia, anorexia nervosa)
• **Bipolar disorder**
• **Abrupt withdrawal from alcohol or benzodiazepines**
• **MAOI** use within 14 days; severe hepatic cirrhosis
• Per lecture: not in **pregnancy, breastfeeding or under 18**
cards.m: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold – anything that already lowers it is a no.

cards.q: What is the seizure risk with bupropion and which factors increase it?
cards.a:
• About **1 in 1,000**
• Risk increased by: **alcohol misuse**, head trauma, **diabetes treated with insulin or sulfonylureas**, stimulants/anorectics
• Drugs lowering seizure threshold: **antipsychotics, antidepressants, tramadol, theophylline, systemic steroids**, antimalarials
• If risk factors present: avoid, or use maximum 150 mg/day

cards.q: In which smokers does bupropion offer particular advantages?
cards.a:
• Smokers **concerned about weight gain** – bupropion **delays** post-cessation weight gain
• Smokers with a history of **depression** (without contraindications)
• Those who prefer a tablet to NRT or cannot tolerate varenicline
cards.m: Bupropion: mood and weight friendly – seizure unfriendly.

cards.q: Why should blood pressure be monitored on bupropion?
cards.a:
• Bupropion can **raise blood pressure**
• Risk is higher when **combined with the nicotine patch**
• Check BP at baseline and during follow-up

cards.q: Which important drug interaction does bupropion have via CYP2D6?
cards.a:
• Bupropion is a **strong CYP2D6 inhibitor**
• Raises levels of CYP2D6 substrates: **tricyclic antidepressants**, some **SSRIs**, **antipsychotics**, **beta-blockers** (e.g. metoprolol), flecainide
• Reduces activation of **tamoxifen** – avoid in women on tamoxifen
cards.m: Bupropion blocks 2D6 – check every 2D6 drug.

cards.q: What is nortriptyline's role in smoking cessation?
cards.a:
• A **tricyclic antidepressant**
• **Reduces tobacco withdrawal symptoms**
• A **second-line** option when first-line agents fail or are unsuitable (off-label)
cards.m: Nortriptyline = the old reserve player.

cards.q: How is nortriptyline started and how long is it given?
cards.a:
• Start about **1 week before the quit date** (some regimens 10–28 days)
• Start low (about 25 mg daily) and titrate to 75–100 mg daily
• Use for **12 weeks**
cards.m: Nortriptyline: like bupropion, start before; like varenicline, 12 weeks.

cards.q: What are the adverse effects of nortriptyline?
cards.a:
• Common: **dry mouth**, **drowsiness** (sedation)
• Anticholinergic: constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention
• **Cardiac arrhythmias**, postural hypotension
• **Dangerous in overdose**
cards.m: Nortriptyline = Dry and Drowsy.

cards.q: Who should not use nortriptyline for smoking cessation?
cards.a:
• **Pregnant** and **breastfeeding** women; **under 18 years** (per lecture)
• **Recent MI**, **arrhythmias** or heart block
• Patients at risk of **overdose/suicide**
• Caution with urinary retention, glaucoma

cards.q: Which smoking cessation drugs are first-line and which are second-line?
cards.a:
• **First-line**: **NRT** (all forms), **varenicline**, **bupropion SR**
• **Second-line**: **nortriptyline** (clonidine elsewhere)
• Most effective options: **varenicline** and **combination NRT**
cards.m: First team: NRT, varenicline, bupropion. Bench: nortriptyline.

cards.q: When is each pharmacotherapy started relative to the quit date?
cards.a:
• **NRT** – **on the quit date** (or earlier when cutting down to quit)
• **Varenicline** – **1–2 weeks before**
• **Bupropion** – **at least 1 week before**
• **Nortriptyline** – about **1 week before**
cards.m: Only nicotine starts on the day; the three tablets start a week or more early.

cards.q: Compare the treatment durations of NRT, varenicline, bupropion and nortriptyline.
cards.a:
• **NRT** – **8–12 weeks** (longer if needed)
• **Varenicline** – **12 weeks** (+12 more if quit)
• **Bupropion** – **at least 7 weeks**
• **Nortriptyline** – **12 weeks**
cards.m: Everything is about 12 weeks – except bupropion's minimum of 7.

cards.q: Match the typical adverse effect to the drug: nausea; insomnia with seizure risk; drowsiness with dry mouth.
cards.a:
• **Nausea** (plus vivid dreams) → **varenicline**
• **Insomnia, dry mouth, headache; seizure risk** → **bupropion**
• **Drowsiness, dry mouth**; arrhythmia → **nortriptyline**
cards.m: V = Vomit, B = Brain buzz (awake, fits), N = Nod off.

cards.q: Which special populations need a tailored approach to smoking cessation?
cards.a:
• **Pregnant and lactating women**
• **Psychiatric patients**
• **Adolescents**
• **Elderly patients**
cards.m: PPAE: Pregnant, Psychiatric, Adolescent, Elderly.

cards.q: What is the first-line approach for pregnant and breastfeeding women who smoke?
cards.a:
• **Multi-session behavioural smoking cessation interventions** for **all** pregnant and breastfeeding smokers
• Ask at booking and every antenatal visit; include partner and household
cards.m: In pregnancy, talk first – multiple sessions.

cards.q: Which non-nicotine pharmacotherapies cannot be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
cards.a:
• **Varenicline**, **bupropion** and **nortriptyline** – all not for pregnant or breastfeeding women
• So **NRT** is the only pharmacological option if behavioural support alone fails
cards.m: In pregnancy, the only drug on the table is nicotine itself.

cards.q: If a pregnant woman cannot stop with behavioural support alone, how should NRT be used?
cards.a:
• NRT may be used after discussing risks and benefits – **safer than smoking**
• Prefer **intermittent short-acting** forms (gum, lozenge, inhaler, spray) to limit total fetal exposure
• If a patch is needed, **remove it at bedtime** (16-hour use)
cards.m: Pregnancy NRT: short, intermittent, and patch off at night.

cards.q: Why is it worth quitting even late in pregnancy, and when is the benefit greatest?
cards.a:
• Quitting at **any stage** improves fetal growth and reduces risk
• Stopping **early (ideally before about 15 weeks)** brings risks of **preterm birth and low birth weight** close to those of non-smokers
• Quitting also reduces the infant's risk of **SIDS**
cards.m: Early quit, normal baby weight.

cards.q: How should smoking cessation be approached in a patient with a psychiatric illness?
cards.a:
• **Record smoking status**, preferably with **FTND** and **CO analyser**
• Provide **5A** intervention
• **Set the quit date when mental status is stable**
• **Offer pharmacotherapy to all** (NRT, bupropion, nortriptyline, varenicline), monitoring neuropsychiatric symptoms – especially with varenicline and bupropion
• Provide behavioural support where available
• Note: slide p54's caution line is garbled ('varencline'); the intended message is above
cards.m: Stable mind first, then the quit date.

cards.q: Does stopping smoking worsen mental health in people with psychiatric illness?
cards.a:
• **No** – quitting is associated with **improved anxiety, depression and stress**
• People with mental illness smoke more heavily and **die 10–20 years earlier**, much of it from smoking
• They are as motivated to quit as others and should be offered full support
cards.m: Smoking does not calm the mind – it just relieves its own withdrawal.

cards.q: Can varenicline or bupropion be used in a smoker with a stable psychiatric illness (e.g. treated depression or schizophrenia)?
cards.a:
• **Yes** – pharmacotherapy should be offered to all smokers with psychiatric conditions
• The EAGLES trial (2016) found no significant increase in serious neuropsychiatric events with varenicline or bupropion versus placebo in this group
• Still **monitor mood and behaviour** at each review and coordinate with the psychiatric team
• Bupropion: check seizure risk and drug interactions (antipsychotics, antidepressants)
cards.m: Mental illness is a reason for closer follow-up, not for withholding treatment.

cards.q: Why do clozapine and olanzapine levels rise when a patient stops smoking?
cards.a:
• **Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons** in tobacco **smoke** (not nicotine) **induce CYP1A2**
• On quitting, induction wears off over about a week → clozapine/olanzapine levels **rise markedly**
• Risk: sedation, hypersalivation, hypotension, **seizures**
• **NRT does not prevent this** – reduce the dose and monitor levels with the psychiatry team
cards.m: It is the smoke, not the nicotine, that speeds up CYP1A2.

cards.q: Besides antipsychotics, which drugs need review when a patient stops smoking?
cards.a:
• **Theophylline/aminophylline** – risk of toxicity
• **Caffeine** – levels rise
• **Warfarin** – monitor INR
• **Insulin** – requirements may change
• Others metabolised by **CYP1A2** (e.g. fluvoxamine, ropinirole)
cards.m: Theo, Coffee, Clozapine, Warfarin – the CYP1A2 quit-check list.

cards.q: What is the first-line approach for adolescent smokers?
cards.a:
• **Counselling and behavioural interventions**
• Involve family/school support; address peer influence and vaping
cards.m: Teens: talk before tablets.

cards.q: When can pharmacotherapy be considered for adolescent smokers?
cards.a:
• When there is **evidence of nicotine dependence** and a **desire to quit**
• **NRT** is the usual option (bupropion SR is mentioned on slide p55)
• **Varenicline is not for under-18s**
• Note: slide p49 states bupropion cannot be used under 18 while slide p55 lists it for adolescents – NRT is the safer choice

cards.q: Is it worth helping elderly smokers to quit?
cards.a:
• **Yes** – cessation **reduces the excess risk of cardiovascular events and mortality even at older age**
• Quitting also slows lung function decline and improves wound healing and surgical outcomes
cards.m: Never too old to quit.

cards.q: Which interventions are effective in elderly smokers?
cards.a:
• **Counselling**, **physician advice**
• **Buddy support** programmes
• **Age-tailored self-help materials**
• **Telephone counselling**
• **Nicotine patch**; NRT increases cessation success

cards.q: What is an e-cigarette and what are its components?
cards.a:
• A **handheld device** that delivers nicotine or other chemicals by **aerosolisation**
• Components: **aerosol generator** (heating coil/atomiser), **battery**, **solution storage area** (cartridge/tank)

cards.q: What does e-cigarette liquid contain?
cards.a:
• **Propylene glycol** and **glycerol** (the base)
• **Nicotine** (variable, sometimes very high, e.g. nicotine salts)
• **Flavourings**
• Stored in **disposable or refillable** cartridges
cards.m: PG + VG + nicotine + flavour.

cards.q: What harms can inhaling e-cigarette aerosol cause?
cards.a:
• Acute effects of **nicotine, flavourants, chemicals** and particulates
• **Accidental nicotine overdose** (e.g. children swallowing e-liquid)
• **Developmental effects on the adolescent brain**
• Uptake of **illicit drug use**
• **Negative psychosocial health**
• **Battery explosion** and burns
cards.m: Vapour is not just water.

cards.q: What is meant by the 'gateway' and 'dual use' concerns with e-cigarettes?
cards.a:
• **Gateway** – young people who vape are more likely to start **conventional cigarettes**
• **Dual use** – many adults use **both** e-cigarettes and cigarettes, so harm is not reduced and nicotine dependence is maintained
cards.m: Vape as a bridge – too often to the cigarette, not away from it.

cards.q: What is the case definition of EVALI?
cards.a:
• **E-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury**
• Use of e-cigarettes **within 90 days** before symptom onset
• **Pulmonary infiltrates** on imaging (e.g. bilateral ground-glass opacities)
• **No other plausible cause** (infection excluded)
cards.m: EVALI: vaped within 90 days + infiltrates + nothing else explains it.

cards.q: What is the epidemiology of EVALI in the USA and Malaysia?
cards.a:
• Large case series first reported in the **USA in 2019**
• By **2020**: **2,807 cases** and **68 deaths** reported to the CDC
• Malaysia: **17 EVALI cases** recorded up to **June 2023**

cards.q: What is the main cause of EVALI and how does it present and get managed?
cards.a:
• Strongly linked to **vitamin E acetate**, an additive in **THC (cannabis)-containing** vaping liquids
• Presentation: cough, breathlessness, chest pain **plus GI symptoms** (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) and **fever**, weight loss; hypoxia
• Diagnosis of exclusion; refer to hospital – **stop vaping**, supportive care, often **systemic corticosteroids**
cards.m: Vitamin E is good to eat, deadly to vape.

cards.q: Should e-cigarettes be recommended as a smoking cessation aid in Malaysia?
cards.a:
• **No** – they are **not an approved smoking cessation therapy** in Malaysia and are not recommended in the MOH CPG
• Offer **evidence-based** treatment: behavioural support plus NRT, varenicline or bupropion
• Risk of **dual use** and continued nicotine dependence
cards.m: Swap the stick for a proven medicine, not a vape.

cards.q: What did the 1995 Muzakarah of the National Fatwa Committee decide about smoking?
cards.a:
• The **37th Muzakarah (1995)** of the Fatwa Committee of the National Council of Islamic Religious Affairs Malaysia decided that **smoking is forbidden (haram)**
• Useful as a culturally relevant motivator for Muslim patients

cards.q: What is the Malaysian fatwa ruling on e-cigarettes and vaping?
cards.a: • In **2015**, the Muzakarah of the National Fatwa Committee decided that **smoking e-cigarettes or vapour is prohibited (haram)**

cards.q: How do heated tobacco products differ from e-cigarettes, and are they a safer way to quit?
cards.a:
• **Heated tobacco products** (e.g. IQOS) heat real **tobacco leaf** to about **350 °C** without burning it
• **E-cigarettes** heat a **liquid** (propylene glycol, glycerol, nicotine, flavours) – no tobacco leaf
• Both deliver **addictive nicotine** plus toxicants; neither is proven safe
• Neither is a recommended cessation aid in Malaysia – offer behavioural support plus NRT, varenicline or bupropion
cards.m: Heat-not-burn is still tobacco – 'no smoke' does not mean 'no harm'

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old taxi driver attends a Klinik Kesihatan for a BSSK health screening. He has smoked 15 cigarettes a day since the age of 15 and is still smoking. The medical officer wants to document his cumulative tobacco exposure before deciding on lung cancer screening eligibility.
What is his smoking history in pack-years?
o: 20 pack-years
40 pack-years
30 pack-years
60 pack-years
15 pack-years
mcq.e: Pack-years = (cigarettes per day ÷ 20) × years smoked. He has smoked for 40 years at 0.75 pack per day, giving 30 pack-years. The common trap is to multiply cigarettes by years without dividing by 20, or to forget to calculate the years from age at onset.
w: Wrong - 20 pack-years would need only about 27 years at this rate.
Wrong - 40 is the number of years smoked, not pack-years.
Correct - (15 ÷ 20) × 40 years = 30 pack-years.
Wrong - 60 pack-years would mean a full 1.5 packs a day for 40 years.
Wrong - 15 is the age he started, not his exposure.

mcq.stem:
Dr Aina, a medical officer at a Klinik Kesihatan, starts asking every adult in the outpatient clinic about tobacco use and enrols those who are willing into the clinic's quit smoking service, where they receive counselling and pharmacotherapy.
Under the WHO FCTC MPOWER package, which component is she delivering?
o: Offer help to quit tobacco use
Monitor tobacco use and prevention policies
Protect people from tobacco smoke
Warn about the dangers of tobacco
Enforce bans on tobacco advertising
mcq.e: Healthcare providers are responsible for the 'O' of MPOWER – Offer help to quit, delivered through brief intervention, quit clinics and medication. Asking about tobacco use in a clinic is part of the cessation process, not population surveillance ('Monitor'), which is done through surveys such as NHMS.
w: Correct - providing cessation support is the 'O' component, the healthcare provider's role.
Wrong - 'Monitor' refers to population surveillance such as NHMS, not individual clinic care.
Wrong - 'Protect' refers to smoke-free laws for public places.
Wrong - 'Warn' refers to mass media campaigns and pictorial health warnings on packs.
Wrong - 'Enforce' is a regulatory measure against tobacco marketing.

mcq.stem:
A family medicine specialist in a district health office is preparing a talk for Klinik Kesihatan staff on why every consultation should include tobacco screening. She reviews the National Health and Morbidity Survey 2019 data on adult smokers.
Which statement about smoking in Malaysia is accurate according to NHMS 2019?
o: About 40% of all Malaysian adults are current smokers
About 10% of Malaysian women are current smokers
About 1 million Malaysians aged 15 and above smoke
Most current smokers had tried to quit at least once in the past year
Fewer than half of current smokers tried to quit last year
mcq.e: NHMS 2019 found 21.3% current smokers (about 4.8 million people aged 15 and above), 40.5% of men and 1.2% of women, and less than half of current smokers had attempted to quit in the previous 12 months. The low quit-attempt rate is the reason clinicians must ask and advise opportunistically. The 40% figure applies to men only.
w: Wrong - about 40% (40.5%) is the prevalence in men; overall it was 21.3%.
Wrong - female prevalence was only about 1.2%.
Wrong - about 4.8 million Malaysians aged 15 and above smoke.
Wrong - less than half attempted to quit in the last 12 months.
Correct - less than half of current smokers attempted to quit in the previous 12 months.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old lorry driver who smokes 40 cigarettes a day attends a Klinik Kesihatan for a routine review. He has no snoring or daytime sleepiness, no splenomegaly and no itch after bathing. BMI 23 kg/m². SpO2 98% on air. FBC: Hb 18.4 g/dL, haematocrit 0.55, normal white cell and platelet counts.
What is the most likely explanation for his raised haemoglobin?
o: Polycythaemia vera from an acquired JAK2 mutation
Secondary polycythaemia from carboxyhaemoglobin-induced hypoxia
Relative polycythaemia from reduced plasma volume with dehydration
Erythropoietin secretion from an occult renal cell carcinoma
Nocturnal hypoxia from undiagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea
mcq.e: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin about 200–250 times more avidly than oxygen, causing tissue hypoxia and a compensatory secondary polycythaemia in heavy smokers. Pulse oximetry cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin, so a normal SpO2 does not exclude it. Isolated raised Hb with normal white cells and platelets and no splenomegaly argues against polycythaemia vera; cessation usually normalises the count.
w: Wrong - polycythaemia vera usually raises white cells and platelets too, often with splenomegaly and aquagenic itch.
Correct - heavy smoking raises carboxyhaemoglobin, causing hypoxia-driven erythropoietin release.
Wrong - nothing suggests dehydration, and relative polycythaemia would not explain a smoker's typical picture.
Wrong - possible but far less likely; smoking is the obvious, common cause here.
Wrong - he has no snoring, sleepiness or obesity to suggest sleep apnoea.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old man who smokes 25 cigarettes a day presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with a painful ulcer on the tip of his right big toe and cold, painful fingers in the cold. He has no diabetes; his lipid profile and blood pressure are normal. Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are absent on the right.
Which intervention is most important to halt progression of his disease?
o: Start aspirin and high-intensity atorvastatin
Refer for an early below-knee amputation
Start cilostazol to improve claudication distance
Complete and permanent smoking cessation
Prescribe oral antibiotics and daily dressings
