mcq.e: A young male heavy smoker without other atherosclerotic risk factors, with distal limb ischaemia, digital ulceration and Raynaud-like symptoms, suggests thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease). Complete cessation of all tobacco is the only intervention proven to halt progression; continued smoking leads to amputation. Antiplatelets and vasodilators are adjuncts only.
w: Wrong - antiplatelet and statin therapy do not halt this inflammatory small-vessel disease.
Wrong - amputation is the outcome to prevent; cessation may save the limb.
Wrong - cilostazol is a symptomatic adjunct at best.
Correct - total smoking cessation is the only measure that stops progression of Buerger's disease.
Wrong - wound care helps the ulcer but not the underlying vasculitis.

mcq.stem:
A 37-year-old woman attends a Klinik Kesihatan family planning clinic requesting the combined oral contraceptive pill. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day and is not ready to quit. BP 124/78 mmHg, BMI 24 kg/m², no migraine and no history of venous thromboembolism.
What is the most appropriate contraceptive advice?
o: Advise against the COC and offer a progestogen-only method or LARC
Prescribe a low-dose 20 microgram ethinylestradiol COC
Prescribe the COC as her blood pressure is within normal limits
Prescribe the COC once she has cut down to 10 cigarettes daily
Prescribe the COC with yearly lipid profile and blood pressure monitoring
mcq.e: Under UKMEC, a woman aged 35 or older who smokes 15 or more cigarettes a day is UKMEC 4 for combined hormonal contraception – an unacceptable arterial thrombotic risk. Cutting down to fewer than 15 a day only moves her to UKMEC 3, where risks still usually outweigh benefits. Offer progestogen-only methods or LARC and offer cessation support.
w: Correct - age 35 or older with 15 or more cigarettes a day is UKMEC 4; offer POP, implant, injectable or IUD.
Wrong - a lower oestrogen dose does not remove the unacceptable risk.
Wrong - normal BP does not offset the risk from age plus heavy smoking.
Wrong - smoking under 15 a day at 35 or older is still UKMEC 3, generally not recommended.
Wrong - monitoring does not make a UKMEC 4 method acceptable.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan. He is listed for an elective inguinal hernia repair at the district hospital in 3 months and asks when he should stop smoking.
What is the best advice?
o: Stop smoking on the morning of the operation
Stop smoking 24 hours before the operation
Stop now, ideally at least 4–8 weeks before surgery
Stop smoking only after the surgical wound has fully healed
Cut down to 5 cigarettes a day in the week before surgery
mcq.e: Stopping at least 4 weeks, and preferably 6–8 weeks, before surgery reduces wound infection, wound dehiscence and cardiopulmonary complications. Any abstinence helps (carbon monoxide clears within a day), but the greatest benefit needs several weeks. He should remain smoke-free through recovery.
w: Wrong - too late to gain wound-healing and respiratory benefits.
Wrong - clears carbon monoxide but gives little benefit for wound and lung complications.
Correct - at least 4 weeks, ideally 6–8 weeks, before surgery gives the greatest reduction in complications.
Wrong - smoking during healing increases wound infection and dehiscence.
Wrong - cutting down briefly gives minimal benefit; complete cessation is advised.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man with hypertension attends his Klinik Kesihatan review. He stopped smoking exactly 12 months ago after 20 years of smoking a pack a day, and asks how much his risk of coronary heart disease has changed.
What is the most accurate answer?
o: Already equal to that of a lifelong non-smoker
No different from that of someone still smoking
Reduced by only about 10% compared with a smoker
About half that of a continuing smoker
Reduced to about one tenth of a smoker's risk
mcq.e: After 1 year of abstinence, the excess risk of coronary heart disease is about half that of a continuing smoker; after about 15 years it approaches that of a never-smoker. Cardiovascular benefits begin within hours (heart rate, BP, carbon monoxide), which makes them powerful motivators to share with patients.
w: Wrong - CHD risk approaches that of a non-smoker only after about 15 years.
Wrong - benefit begins quickly; by 1 year the excess risk is substantially lower.
Wrong - this underestimates the benefit; the excess risk is about halved.
Correct - at 1 year, CHD risk is about half that of a continuing smoker.
Wrong - this overstates the 1-year benefit.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man with ulcerative colitis has been in remission on mesalazine for 5 years. He stopped smoking 6 weeks ago with NRT support at a Klinik Kesihatan. He now has 6 loose stools a day with blood for 1 week. He is afebrile, pulse 88/min, abdomen soft.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Advise him to resume smoking to control the colitis
Use high-dose nicotine gum as treatment for the colitis
Reassure him that these are nicotine withdrawal symptoms
Treat the colitis flare and support continued abstinence
Stop mesalazine and repeat colonoscopy in 12 months
mcq.e: Ulcerative colitis is the notable exception in which smoking appears protective, and some patients flare after quitting. This is never a reason to resume smoking, because the overall harms far outweigh any colonic effect. Assess severity, treat the flare (and involve gastroenterology as needed) while continuing cessation support.
w: Wrong - the harms of smoking vastly outweigh any benefit in ulcerative colitis.
Wrong - nicotine is not a recommended treatment for UC flares.
Wrong - bloody diarrhoea is not a feature of nicotine withdrawal.
Correct - manage the flare on its merits and keep him smoke-free.
Wrong - stopping maintenance therapy during a flare is inappropriate.

mcq.stem:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan with his fourth episode of acute otitis media this year and recurrent wheeze. His father smokes 15 cigarettes a day, usually in the living room with the windows open, and sometimes in the car.
What is the most appropriate advice to the father about his smoking?
o: Smoke only beside an open window or under a fan
Keep the home and car completely smoke-free
Smoke only in a separate room with the door closed
Run an air purifier in the child's bedroom at night
Switch to e-cigarettes when smoking inside the house
mcq.e: Second-hand smoke increases otitis media, asthma, lower respiratory tract infections and sudden infant death syndrome in children. There is no safe level of exposure, and ventilation, fans, purifiers and separate rooms do not remove the risk. Advise a completely smoke-free home and car, and offer the father cessation support.
w: Wrong - ventilation does not remove second-hand smoke exposure.
Correct - only a completely smoke-free home and car protects the child; also offer help to quit.
Wrong - smoke and residues spread through the house.
Wrong - air purifiers do not remove the risk.
Wrong - e-cigarette aerosol also exposes children to nicotine and chemicals.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man started 4 mg nicotine gum for cravings 1 week ago at a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic. He chews the gum correctly but usually does so while drinking his morning coffee and afternoon cola. He says the gum 'does nothing' for his cravings.
What best explains the poor effect?
o: Caffeine blocks nicotinic receptors in the brain
Coffee speeds hepatic metabolism of nicotine
The 4 mg gum strength is too high for him
Drinking while chewing makes him swallow most of the released nicotine
Acidic drinks ionise nicotine, cutting buccal uptake
mcq.e: Nicotine is a weak base (pKa 8.0) and is absorbed across the buccal mucosa only in its un-ionised form. Acidic drinks such as coffee, cola and juice lower oral pH, ionising nicotine and reducing absorption from gum and lozenges. Advise avoiding acidic drinks for 15 minutes before and during use.
w: Wrong - caffeine does not block nicotinic receptors.
Wrong - the problem is absorption in the mouth, not liver metabolism.
Wrong - a dose that is too high would cause nicotine excess, not lack of effect.
Wrong - swallowing occurs with fast chewing, but the key mechanism here is pH.
Correct - low oral pH ionises nicotine and limits buccal absorption.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man in a workplace quit programme says he has not smoked at all for a week. His colleague reports seeing him smoke about 48 hours ago. He uses no NRT or e-cigarettes. The clinic wants a test that would still show nicotine intake from 2 days ago.
Which test is most appropriate?
o: Plasma nicotine level
Salivary cotinine level
Exhaled carbon monoxide
Blood carboxyhaemoglobin
Urinary nicotine level
mcq.e: Nicotine has a half-life of about 2 hours, so it is cleared within hours, and carbon monoxide clears within about a day. Cotinine, the main metabolite (70–80% of nicotine), has a half-life of about 16–20 hours and stays detectable for several days, making it the preferred biomarker. Its limitation is that NRT and e-cigarette users also test positive.
w: Wrong - nicotine's half-life of about 2 hours means it is undetectable after 48 hours.
Correct - cotinine (half-life about 16–20 hours) remains detectable for several days.
Wrong - exhaled CO reflects smoking only over roughly the past day.
Wrong - carboxyhaemoglobin falls to normal within about 12–24 hours.
Wrong - nicotine itself is cleared too quickly to detect after 2 days.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old university student who smokes 10 cigarettes a day attends a Klinik Kesihatan. He says he only smokes 'for fun' and cannot understand why he feels irritable and craves a cigarette whenever he tries to stop.
Which mechanism best explains his nicotine dependence?
o: α4β2 nicotinic receptors driving dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens
Muscarinic M1 receptors driving acetylcholine release in the frontal cortex
μ-opioid receptors driving β-endorphin release in the hypothalamic nuclei
GABA-A receptors driving serotonin release in the dorsal raphe nuclei
NMDA receptors driving noradrenaline release in the locus coeruleus
mcq.e: Nicotine binds α4β2 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the ventral tegmental area, triggering dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens (mesolimbic reward pathway). Repeated use causes tolerance, and stopping causes withdrawal, driving relapse. Varenicline is a partial agonist at exactly this receptor.
w: Correct - α4β2 nicotinic receptor stimulation releases dopamine in the reward pathway.
Wrong - nicotine acts on nicotinic, not muscarinic, receptors.
Wrong - β-endorphin release is a secondary effect, not the core addiction mechanism.
Wrong - nicotine does not act primarily through GABA-A receptors.
Wrong - noradrenaline release contributes to arousal, not the core reward.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old woman who stopped smoking 3 months ago with varenicline attends a Klinik Kesihatan follow-up. She has gained 4 kg and is tempted to start smoking again. TSH and fasting glucose are normal and she has no oedema.
What best explains her weight gain?
o: Fluid retention caused by nicotine withdrawal
Hypothyroidism unmasked by stopping smoking
A metabolic adverse effect of varenicline
Loss of nicotine's appetite suppression and metabolic boost
Insulin resistance and fluid shifts caused by carbon monoxide clearance
mcq.e: Nicotine suppresses appetite (via noradrenaline and serotonin) and increases metabolic rate. On quitting, appetite rises and energy expenditure falls, giving an average gain of about 4–5 kg in the first year. Reassure that this is far less harmful than smoking, and plan diet and exercise rather than relapse.
w: Wrong - withdrawal does not cause fluid retention, and she has no oedema.
Wrong - TSH is normal.
Wrong - varenicline does not cause weight gain; it is from stopping nicotine.
Correct - losing nicotine's appetite suppression and metabolic boost causes post-cessation weight gain.
Wrong - quitting improves insulin sensitivity over time.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man at a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic is reluctant to start nicotine gum. He says, 'I will just swap one addiction for another – nicotine is nicotine.'
Which explanation best addresses his concern?
o: Medicinal nicotine is chemically different from tobacco nicotine
Gum contains a nicotine antagonist that blocks the reward
Gum gives slower absorption and lower peaks than an inhaled puff
Gum nicotine is fully broken down before it can reach the brain
Gum nicotine bypasses the nicotinic receptors in the brain
mcq.e: Inhaled nicotine reaches the brain in about 11 seconds as a high arterial bolus, giving an immediate reward linked to each puff, which drives addiction. NRT delivers nicotine more slowly and at lower peaks, so it is far less reinforcing, and long-term NRT dependence is uncommon and far safer than smoking.
w: Wrong - the nicotine molecule is the same.
Wrong - NRT contains no antagonist; that is part of varenicline's action.
Correct - slow absorption and lower peak levels make NRT much less addictive.
Wrong - NRT nicotine does reach the brain; that is how it relieves withdrawal.
Wrong - it acts on the same receptors, which is why it reduces cravings.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with stable angina smokes 20 cigarettes a day. At his Klinik Kesihatan review he asks why his chest pain is more frequent on days when he smokes heavily.
Which effect of nicotine best explains this?
o: Coronary vasodilation that lowers coronary perfusion pressure on exertion
Coronary vasoconstriction with a rise in heart rate and BP
Bradycardia with a fall in cardiac output
Hypotension caused by adrenal medulla suppression
Direct myocardial toxicity of the metabolite cotinine
mcq.e: Nicotine stimulates the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal catecholamine release, increasing heart rate, cardiac output and blood pressure (raising myocardial oxygen demand) while causing coronary vasoconstriction (reducing supply). Carbon monoxide further lowers oxygen delivery. This supply–demand mismatch provokes angina.
w: Wrong - nicotine constricts, not dilates, coronary arteries.
Correct - more oxygen demand plus coronary vasoconstriction provokes ischaemia.
Wrong - nicotine causes tachycardia and raises cardiac output.
Wrong - nicotine stimulates the adrenal medulla and raises BP.
Wrong - cotinine is not significantly cardiotoxic.

mcq.stem:
A medical officer at a busy Klinik Kesihatan sees 80 patients a day. A 48-year-old man attending for a sore throat smokes 20 cigarettes a day. The doctor has about 3 minutes left and has not been trained to run a cessation programme. The clinic has a quit smoking service on Thursdays.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: Defer the subject until he raises smoking himself
Advise him to cut down to 5 cigarettes a day
Prescribe varenicline today and review him in 3 months' time
Ask, give brief advice and refer to the quit service
Hand him a leaflet only, as advice takes too long
mcq.e: The ABC (Ask, Brief advice, Cessation support) approach suits busy clinicians: ask and document smoking status, give personalised brief advice, then either provide support or refer to a cessation service if lacking time or expertise. Even advice lasting under 3 minutes increases quit rates, so no smoker should leave without an offer of help.
w: Wrong - every smoker should be asked and advised at every opportunity.
Wrong - cutting down without a plan is not the recommended advice.
Wrong - prescribing without assessment, counselling and early follow-up is poor practice.
Correct - ABC: ask, brief advice and refer when lacking time or expertise.
Wrong - a leaflet alone is less effective than brief advice plus referral.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man with asthma attends a Klinik Kesihatan after a mild exacerbation. When asked about smoking he says, 'I know smoking is making my asthma worse and I do want to stop one day, but I have not thought about how or when.'
Which stage of change is he in?
o: Precontemplation
Preparation
Contemplation
Action
Maintenance
mcq.e: In contemplation the person recognises the problem and intends to change within about 6 months but has no plan yet and is ambivalent. Precontemplation lacks awareness or intention; preparation involves concrete plans within 30 days. Contemplators benefit from the 5R and motivational interviewing to resolve ambivalence.
w: Wrong - he recognises the problem and wants to stop, so he is past precontemplation.
Wrong - preparation requires concrete plans, such as a quit date within 30 days.
Correct - aware of the problem, wants to stop, but no plan yet.
Wrong - action means he has already stopped smoking.
Wrong - maintenance means abstinence for more than 6 months.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old man tells the Klinik Kesihatan doctor that he has thrown away his ashtrays, told his wife he is quitting and wants to stop next week before his daughter's wedding. He smokes 18 cigarettes a day, with his first cigarette 20 minutes after waking.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Explore relevance and risks using the 5R approach
Congratulate him on his plan and discuss relapse prevention only
Advise him to return when he feels completely ready
Give leaflets and repeat the advice at his next visit
Set a quit date and offer pharmacotherapy with support
mcq.e: He is in the preparation stage – making concrete plans and intending to quit within 30 days. The matching intervention is 'Assist': set a quit date (STAR), offer pharmacotherapy and behavioural support, and arrange follow-up. The 5R is for smokers unwilling to quit, and relapse prevention alone suits maintenance.
w: Wrong - the 5R is for smokers unwilling to quit; he is already motivated.
Wrong - relapse prevention alone suits the maintenance stage.
Wrong - he is ready now; delaying wastes the opportunity.
Wrong - he needs active assistance now, not just repeated advice.
Correct - preparation stage: STAR quit date plus pharmacotherapy and support.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old man who smokes 15 cigarettes a day agrees to quit after brief advice at a Klinik Kesihatan. The doctor uses the STAR method to plan the attempt with him.
Within what time frame should his quit date be set?
o: Within the next 2 weeks
Within the next 3 months
Within the next 6 months
After his next annual review
Once he is down to 5 a day
mcq.e: STAR = Set a quit date (within 2 weeks), Tell family, friends and co-workers, Anticipate challenges including withdrawal, and Remove tobacco products. A date within 2 weeks keeps motivation high while allowing preparation and pre-loading of varenicline or bupropion.
w: Correct - STAR sets a quit date within 2 weeks.
Wrong - a date this far away lets motivation fade.
Wrong - 6 months matches the contemplation stage, not a set quit date.
Wrong - delaying until an annual review loses the moment of readiness.
Wrong - cutting down first is not the STAR step and delays quitting.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old man with type 2 diabetes sets his quit date for next Monday at a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic and starts varenicline today. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and has relapsed twice before within the first few days.
When should his first follow-up after the quit date be arranged?
o: One month after the quit date
Within the first week after the quit date
Three months after the quit date
At his next routine diabetes review in 3 months
Only if he reports a lapse or a relapse
mcq.e: The recommended schedule is a follow-up in the first week after the quit date, weekly during the first month, every 2 weeks in months 2–3, then monthly up to 6 months. Withdrawal peaks and relapse risk is highest in the first days, so early contact (in person, by phone or virtually) allows side effects and dose problems to be handled.
w: Wrong - by 1 month many relapses have already happened.
Correct - first follow-up within the first week after the quit date, when relapse risk is highest.
Wrong - far too late for the high-risk early period.
Wrong - linking it to a routine review delays essential early support.
Wrong - follow-up is proactive, not only after relapse.

mcq.stem:
A 39-year-old woman has been completely abstinent for 6 weeks since her quit date and is taking varenicline without side effects. She has attended weekly Klinik Kesihatan reviews during the first month.
What follow-up schedule is now recommended?
o: Weekly visits until 6 months after the quit date
Monthly visits from now until 1 year
Every 3 months until 1 year after quitting
Every 2 weeks until the end of the third month
No further visits as she has already quit
mcq.e: After weekly reviews in month 1, follow-up is every 2 weeks during months 2 and 3, then monthly up to 6 months. Reviews can be in person, by telephone or virtual, and should check medication use, congratulate success and address any lapses.
w: Wrong - weekly reviews are only for the first month.
Wrong - monthly reviews start after month 3 and run to 6 months.
Wrong - 3-monthly reviews are too infrequent in the early months.
Correct - every 2 weeks in months 2 and 3, then monthly up to 6 months.
Wrong - relapse risk persists; structured follow-up continues to 6 months.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old man using a 21 mg nicotine patch attends a Klinik Kesihatan 3 weeks after his quit date. He admits smoking 3 cigarettes at a friend's wedding last weekend while drinking with old smoking friends, but none since. He feels he has 'failed'.
What is the most appropriate response?
o: Review the trigger, recommit to abstinence and continue NRT
Stop the patch now, as smoking while using it is dangerous
Restart the whole programme with a new quit date in 6 months
Switch straight to varenicline, as NRT has clearly failed him
Advise him to cut down gradually instead of stopping completely
mcq.e: A lapse is not a relapse and not a failure. At follow-up, review the situation (here alcohol and smoking friends), reassess commitment to total abstinence, and continue pharmacotherapy. Smoking while on NRT is not dangerous, and stopping treatment after a single lapse increases the chance of full relapse.
w: Correct - review the circumstances, renew commitment to total abstinence and continue NRT.
Wrong - smoking on NRT is not dangerous; stopping NRT raises relapse risk.
Wrong - an unnecessary delay; he is still motivated now.
Wrong - one trigger-related lapse does not mean NRT has failed.
Wrong - the goal remains total abstinence.

mcq.stem:
A 61-year-old man with hypertension is asked about tobacco use at a Klinik Kesihatan. He says he stopped smoking 3 months ago without any help after 30 years of smoking, and has had no cigarettes since.
What is the most appropriate action?
o: No action is needed, as he no longer smokes
Start varenicline now to prevent any future relapse
Use the 5R approach to strengthen his motivation
Refer him to the quit clinic for a Fagerström test
Congratulate him and discuss relapse prevention
mcq.e: The 'Ask' step has four possible answers: willing smoker, unwilling smoker, ex-smoker or non-smoker. A recent ex-smoker is still at risk of relapse and should be congratulated, have his success reinforced and be helped to identify high-risk situations. Pharmacotherapy and the 5R are for current smokers.
w: Wrong - recent ex-smokers still need reinforcement because relapse risk persists.
Wrong - he is abstinent without withdrawal; medication is not indicated.
Wrong - the 5R is for current smokers unwilling to quit.
Wrong - the FTND assesses dependence in current smokers.
Correct - congratulate, reinforce and give relapse-prevention advice.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old man with chronic stable angina attends a Klinik Kesihatan for his medication refill. He smokes 15 cigarettes a day and has never been advised to quit. The doctor moves to the 'Advise' step of the 5A.
Which approach best fits the recommended way to advise him?
o: Suggest he might cut down a little when convenient for him
Warn him bluntly that he will die soon if he keeps smoking
Clear, strong advice linking quitting to his angina, with help
Avoid the topic, as he came only for his medication refill
Recommend light or menthol cigarettes as a safer alternative
mcq.e: Advice should be clear, strong and personalised – for example, explaining that quitting is the most important thing he can do for his heart and that the clinic will help. Linking advice to the current illness increases its impact. Vague, fear-based or judgemental messages are less effective, and 'light' cigarettes give no benefit because of compensatory smoking.
w: Wrong - vague advice to cut down is weak and unpersonalised.
Wrong - fear-based, confrontational messages provoke resistance.
Correct - clear, strong, personalised advice plus an offer of help.
Wrong - every smoker should be advised at every opportunity.
Wrong - light and menthol cigarettes are not safer.

mcq.stem:
A 37-year-old man preparing to quit tells the Klinik Kesihatan doctor that both of his previous attempts ended at weekend gatherings where he drank beer with friends who smoke.
As part of 'Assist', which advice is most appropriate?
o: Drink only at home rather than at gatherings with friends
Use an e-cigarette whenever he drinks with his friends
Chew nicotine gum only on the nights when he is drinking
Limit or avoid alcohol during the quit attempt
Delay his quit date until he has stopped drinking alcohol
mcq.e: Assist includes exploring past quit experiences and advising the patient to limit or abstain from alcohol, a major relapse trigger. Alcohol lowers inhibition and is often linked to smoking cues. The quit attempt should not be delayed; instead, plan to avoid high-risk settings early on.
w: Wrong - drinking anywhere still weakens resolve and triggers cravings.
Wrong - e-cigarettes are not an approved cessation aid and maintain dependence.
Wrong - NRT should be used regularly, not only on drinking nights.
Correct - limiting or abstaining from alcohol is part of 'Assist'.
Wrong - delaying the quit date loses the current motivation.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old man completes the Fagerström Test at a Klinik Kesihatan. He smokes his first cigarette about 20 minutes after waking and smokes 25 a day. He finds it hard not to smoke in no-smoking areas, and the morning cigarette is the one he would most hate to give up. He does not smoke more in the morning than later in the day and does not smoke when ill in bed.
What is his score and level of dependence?
o: 6 – moderately dependent
7 – highly dependent
5 – moderately dependent
8 – highly dependent
3 – minimally dependent
mcq.e: Scoring: first cigarette 5–30 minutes = 2; 21–30 cigarettes a day = 2; difficult in forbidden places = 1; first morning cigarette most hated to give up = 1; not more in the morning = 0; not when ill = 0. Total 6 = moderately dependent (4–6). Scores of 7–10 are highly dependent and below 4 minimally dependent.
w: Correct - 2 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 6, moderately dependent.
Wrong - 7 would need one more positive item.
Wrong - 5 undercounts his answers by one point; the total is 6.
Wrong - this overcounts the time-to-first-cigarette and per-day items.
Wrong - 3 undercounts his answers.

mcq.stem:
A busy Klinik Kesihatan wants a very short screen for nicotine dependence to decide quickly on pharmacotherapy dose, as the full 6-item Fagerström Test is often skipped.
Which single item is the best predictor of nicotine dependence?
o: Still smoking when ill in bed most of the day
Difficulty not smoking in no-smoking places
Time to the first cigarette after waking
Smoking more in the first hours after waking
Hating most to give up the first cigarette
mcq.e: Time to first cigarette after waking (up to 3 points) is the single strongest predictor of dependence. Together with cigarettes per day it forms the Heaviness of Smoking Index (0–6), a quick screen used to guide NRT strength (for example, 4 mg gum or lozenge if the first cigarette is within 30 minutes).
w: Wrong - scores only 1 point and is a weaker predictor.
Wrong - scores only 1 point.
Correct - time to first cigarette is the strongest single predictor of dependence.
Wrong - scores only 1 point.
Wrong - related, but scores only 1 point and predicts less well.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old woman stopped smoking 3 days ago without medication. She phones the Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic complaining of irritability, poor concentration, restlessness and difficulty sleeping, and asks how long this will last.
What is the most accurate answer?
o: Most will settle within the next 24 hours
Most will be gone by the end of day 3
They usually persist for at least a year
They typically last for about 6 months
Most settle over about 2–4 weeks
mcq.e: Nicotine withdrawal begins within hours, peaks in the first few days and mostly subsides over 2–4 weeks. Increased appetite and cue-triggered cravings can last longer – weeks to months. Explaining this time course helps patients persevere, and pharmacotherapy can reduce symptoms.
w: Wrong - symptoms peak in the first few days rather than settling in 24 hours.
Wrong - day 3 is around the peak, not the end.
Wrong - most symptoms do not last a year; only occasional cravings may persist.
Wrong - 6 months greatly overstates the usual duration.
Correct - withdrawal peaks early and mostly resolves over 2–4 weeks.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man stopped smoking 10 days ago. His irritability and cravings improved by day 7, but he now has palpitations, tremor, anxiety and insomnia. He drinks 6 cups of strong coffee a day, unchanged from before. He uses no NRT or other medication. Pulse 96/min, regular; thyroid examination normal.
What is the most likely explanation?
o: Nicotine withdrawal reaching its peak at day 10
Raised caffeine levels as CYP1A2 induction wanes
Thyrotoxicosis unmasked by stopping smoking
Paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia episodes
Rebound sympathetic overactivity from cotinine
mcq.e: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke induce CYP1A2, which metabolises caffeine. After quitting, this induction wanes and caffeine levels can roughly double on the same intake, causing jitteriness, palpitations and insomnia that mimic withdrawal. Advise halving caffeine intake during the quit attempt.
w: Wrong - withdrawal peaks in the first few days and his had already improved.
Correct - loss of CYP1A2 induction raises caffeine levels on the same intake.
Wrong - quitting does not cause thyrotoxicosis, and his thyroid examination is normal.
Wrong - his pulse is regular at 96/min, not a paroxysmal tachyarrhythmia.
Wrong - cotinine does not cause rebound sympathetic activation.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man stopped smoking 2 weeks ago after 30 pack-years. His cough has become more productive of clear sputum. He has no fever, haemoptysis or weight loss, and chest examination is normal. SpO2 97% on air.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Reassure him that clearance is recovering and review if it persists
Advise him to smoke a few cigarettes each day until the cough settles
Start oral amoxicillin for a presumed chest infection
Arrange an urgent CT thorax for suspected lung cancer
Start an inhaled corticosteroid for new-onset asthma
mcq.e: In the early weeks after quitting, recovering cilia start clearing accumulated mucus, so cough and sputum can temporarily increase. Without red flags, reassure and review; investigate if there is haemoptysis, weight loss, fever or a cough persisting beyond several weeks. This explanation also prevents relapse.
w: Correct - temporary cough from recovering mucociliary clearance; reassure and review.
Wrong - smoking would undo the benefit and is never advised.
Wrong - no fever or focal signs to suggest infection.
Wrong - no red flags; urgent CT is not indicated now.
Wrong - nothing suggests asthma.

mcq.stem:
A 42-year-old man using a 21 mg nicotine patch and gum says he has not smoked for 2 weeks. His wife thinks he still smokes at work. The Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic wants an objective check of whether he is still smoking.
Which test is most appropriate?
o: Urine cotinine level
Salivary cotinine level
Plasma nicotine level
Serum nicotine metabolite ratio
Exhaled carbon monoxide
mcq.e: Exhaled carbon monoxide reflects combustion of tobacco over roughly the past day and is unaffected by NRT, so it can verify abstinence in people using NRT. Cotinine and nicotine are derived from any nicotine source and will be positive in patients on NRT. A CO analyser also motivates patients by showing a visible fall after quitting.
w: Wrong - cotinine will be positive from his NRT.
Wrong - salivary cotinine is also raised by NRT.
Wrong - plasma nicotine reflects his patch and gum.
Wrong - this ratio reflects how fast he metabolises nicotine, not whether he smokes.
Correct - exhaled CO detects smoking and is not raised by NRT.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old contractor with COPD is referred to a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day, the first right after waking. His only previous attempt was 2 days of cold turkey, abandoned because of withdrawal. Fagerström score 9/10. He is worried about withdrawal and unsure about quitting.
What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Try cold turkey again with a firm quit date and leaflets only
Gradual reduction over 6 months without any medication
Nicotine gum 2 mg only when cravings become severe
Varenicline or combination NRT plus behavioural support
Switch to e-cigarettes to taper his nicotine intake
mcq.e: A Fagerström score of 7–10 indicates high dependence, and his early relapse shows withdrawal overwhelmed willpower. The most effective approach is the most effective pharmacotherapy (varenicline or combination NRT: patch plus short-acting form) with behavioural support and close follow-up. Unassisted cold turkey succeeds in only about 3–5%.
w: Wrong - unassisted cold turkey already failed and has very low success.
Wrong - reduction without medication does not address his high dependence.
Wrong - low-dose, as-needed gum alone is insufficient for an FTND of 9.
Correct - high dependence needs varenicline or combination NRT with behavioural support.
Wrong - e-cigarettes are not an approved cessation therapy in Malaysia.

mcq.stem:
A 29-year-old man who quit 5 days ago tells the Klinik Kesihatan nurse that his urges to smoke feel unbearable and he fears they will last all day. The nurse teaches him the 4D technique.
How long does a single strong urge typically last?
o: About 30 seconds
About 30 minutes
About 3 minutes
About 3 hours
About 1 whole day
mcq.e: A single strong urge typically passes in about 3 minutes. Teaching patients to ride it out with the 4D – deep breathing, drink plenty of water, divert thinking and discuss with a friend – builds confidence, and each urge resisted weakens the next.
w: Wrong - urges usually last longer than this.
Wrong - this overstates the length of a single urge.
Correct - a strong urge typically passes within about 3 minutes.
Wrong - a single urge does not last hours.
Wrong - cravings recur, but each urge is brief.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old lorry driver at a Klinik Kesihatan says he is not ready to quit. The doctor asks what makes quitting hard for him. He says all his co-workers smoke and he becomes very moody when he tries to stop. The doctor explains that medication can control the moodiness and suggests ways to cope at work.
Which element of the 5R is being used?
o: Relevance
Roadblocks
Rewards
Risks
Repetition
mcq.e: Roadblocks: ask the patient to identify barriers to quitting, then offer treatment that addresses them (here, pharmacotherapy for withdrawal and strategies for being around smokers). Relevance personalises why quitting matters; Risks and Rewards ask about harms and benefits; Repetition repeats the intervention at every visit.
w: Wrong - Relevance is why quitting matters to him personally.
Correct - identifying barriers and offering solutions is Roadblocks.
Wrong - Rewards are the benefits of stopping.
Wrong - Risks are the negative consequences of smoking.
Wrong - Repetition means repeating the intervention at every visit.

mcq.stem:
A 36-year-old man who is not ready to quit is asked by the Klinik Kesihatan doctor what he might gain if he stopped. He mentions saving money for his children's education, food tasting better and being able to play football again.
Which element of the 5R is being used?
o: Relevance
Risks
Rewards
Roadblocks
Repetition
mcq.e: Rewards: the patient identifies potential benefits of stopping, such as better health, saving money, improved taste and smell, and being a role model. Self-identified benefits are more persuasive than benefits listed by the clinician.
w: Wrong - Relevance links quitting to his own situation, such as illness or family.
Wrong - Risks are the negative consequences of continuing to smoke.
Correct - identifying the benefits of stopping is Rewards.
Wrong - Roadblocks are barriers to quitting.
Wrong - Repetition is repeating the intervention at every visit.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man with hypertension has been given the 5R at a Klinik Kesihatan. He listens politely but firmly says he has no intention of stopping smoking now. His BP is controlled on amlodipine.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Prescribe varenicline anyway so it is ready when he changes his mind
Discharge him from the clinic until he is willing to quit
Withhold his antihypertensive refill until he agrees to quit
Tell him not to discuss smoking again unless he raises it
Respect his choice and revisit motivation at every visit
mcq.e: Repetition: the motivational intervention should be repeated every time an unmotivated patient attends, and each discussion documented. Most smokers need several contacts before they decide to quit. Respecting autonomy keeps the door open; withholding care or prescribing to an unwilling patient is inappropriate.
w: Wrong - pharmacotherapy is for smokers who are ready to make a quit attempt.
Wrong - he still needs care and repeated motivation.
Wrong - unethical and harmful.
Wrong - clinicians should raise it at every visit.
Correct - repeat the 5R at every visit and document.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman who smokes 15 cigarettes a day tells the Klinik Kesihatan doctor she will not quit because she gained weight during a previous attempt. BMI 24 kg/m².
What is the most appropriate response to this roadblock?
o: Agree that she should keep smoking until she reaches her target weight
Explain the modest gain is far less harmful and plan diet and exercise
Start orlistat now so that she loses weight before she quits
Advise a strict very low-calorie diet from her quit date
Recommend menthol cigarettes, which suppress appetite more
mcq.e: Weight gain is a common roadblock. Average gain is about 4–5 kg, and its health effect is far smaller than the harm of continued smoking. Plan healthy eating and physical activity; NRT and bupropion can delay gain. Strict dieting during a quit attempt adds stress and increases relapse risk.
w: Wrong - smoking is never a safe weight-control method.
Correct - put the modest gain in context and plan diet and exercise.
Wrong - weight-loss drugs are not indicated at a BMI of 24.
Wrong - strict dieting during a quit attempt increases relapse.
Wrong - menthol cigarettes are not safer.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man with a chronic cough is not ready to quit. He tells the Klinik Kesihatan doctor, 'My grandfather smoked all his life and lived to 90, so smoking cannot be that bad.'
Which response best follows motivational interviewing principles?
o: You have seen people smoke without harm, yet you are worried about this cough.
Your grandfather was just lucky; the statistics show you will probably die early.
That is simply not true, and I must insist that you stop smoking today.
If you will not listen to medical advice, there is little more I can do.
Let us talk about your cough medicine instead of your smoking then.
mcq.e: Motivational interviewing uses empathy and reflective listening, rolls with resistance rather than arguing, and develops discrepancy between the patient's behaviour and his own concerns or goals. Reflecting his view while linking it to his worry about the cough invites him to explore change. Confrontation increases resistance.
w: Correct - a reflection that rolls with resistance and develops discrepancy.
Wrong - argumentative and fear-based; it provokes resistance.
Wrong - confrontational demands increase resistance.
Wrong - rejecting the patient closes the door to change.
Wrong - avoids the issue and misses the opportunity.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old man says he will not try to quit again because his two attempts using 'willpower alone' failed within a week. He thinks people who quit are simply stronger than him and does not know what else is available.
What is the most appropriate response to this roadblock?
o: Agree that quitting depends mainly on willpower and personality
Advise him to try willpower once more, with a stricter deadline
Suggest he waits until a health scare gives him motivation
Advise him to switch to e-cigarettes as the most effective aid
Explain that medicine plus support greatly improves success
mcq.e: Limited knowledge of effective treatment is a recognised roadblock. Unassisted attempts succeed in only about 3–5%, while pharmacotherapy roughly doubles quit rates and combining it with behavioural support improves them further. Tell him about free help at Klinik Kesihatan quit clinics and mQuit services, and normalise previous failed attempts.
w: Wrong - dependence is a medical condition; willpower alone rarely succeeds.
Wrong - repeating an unassisted attempt has a low success rate.
Wrong - waiting for a health scare risks serious harm.
Wrong - e-cigarettes are not an approved cessation therapy in Malaysia.
Correct - pharmacotherapy plus behavioural support greatly improves success.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old bank officer in Kuala Lumpur sees a private GP for a cough and wants help to stop smoking. The GP has a 5-minute appointment slot and no cessation training. The patient works long hours and cannot attend a government clinic during office hours.
What is the most appropriate referral?
o: Tell him to return when he feels ready to quit on his own
Refer him to a psychiatrist for addiction management
Refer him only to a tertiary hospital respiratory clinic
Advise him to buy e-cigarettes from a vape shop instead
Refer him to an mQuit-registered provider near his workplace
mcq.e: mQuit is the MOH smoking cessation programme linking public and private providers – Klinik Kesihatan, hospitals, private GP clinics and community pharmacies – so smokers can get help near home or work. When the treating clinician lacks time or expertise, referral to a cessation service is the 'C' of the ABC approach.
w: Wrong - motivated smokers should be helped or referred now.
Wrong - uncomplicated tobacco dependence does not need psychiatry.
Wrong - tertiary clinics are not the first port of call and are hard for him to access.
Wrong - e-cigarettes are not an approved cessation therapy in Malaysia.
Correct - mQuit gives access to cessation support through public and private providers.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old man ready to quit is offered varenicline and weekly counselling sessions at a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic. He says he only wants the tablets because he is too busy for counselling.
What is the most accurate advice?
o: Tablets alone are just as effective as tablets with counselling
Counselling alone is better than medication for most smokers
Combining medication with behavioural support works best
Counselling is only needed if the tablets fail after 12 weeks
Medication should be given only to those who fail counselling
mcq.e: Combining behavioural intervention with medication increases the chance of quitting more than either alone. Medication blunts withdrawal, while behavioural support deals with habits, triggers and motivation. All smokers attempting to quit should be offered pharmacotherapy unless contraindicated; counselling can be brief or by phone if time is a barrier.
w: Wrong - adding behavioural support further increases success.
Wrong - medication plus support beats either alone.
Correct - combined behavioural and pharmacological treatment gives the best quit rates.
Wrong - support should be given from the start, not only after failure.
Wrong - pharmacotherapy should be offered to all unless contraindicated.

mcq.stem:
A 33-year-old office worker quit smoking 4 days ago. After lunch he feels a sudden, strong urge to smoke at his desk and phones the Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic counsellor for advice.
Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Smoke just one cigarette to settle the urge, then stop again
Drink water and take slow deep breaths until the urge passes
Drink a cup of strong coffee to take his mind off the urge
Chew ordinary gum vigorously for an hour to distract himself
Have a small alcoholic drink after work to help him relax
mcq.e: The 4D technique – Deep breathing, Drink plenty of water, Divert thinking and Discuss with a friend – helps a person ride out an urge, which usually passes in about 3 minutes. One cigarette often leads to full relapse, and coffee and alcohol are common smoking triggers.
w: Wrong - 'just one' often leads to full relapse.
Correct - deep breathing and drinking water are part of the 4D; the urge passes in minutes.
Wrong - coffee is a common smoking cue and caffeine levels rise after quitting.
Wrong - not a recognised strategy and an hour is unnecessary.
Wrong - alcohol is a major relapse trigger.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old contractor preparing to quit tells the Klinik Kesihatan doctor that his strongest urges come immediately after every meal, when he habitually lights up at the table.
Which behavioural strategy is most appropriate for this trigger?
o: Leave the table straight after meals and brush his teeth
Skip meals during the first month to avoid the trigger
Allow himself one cigarette after dinner as a reward
Eat larger meals so that he feels too full to smoke
Smoke only half a cigarette after each meal for a while
mcq.e: Identify triggers (when, where and with whom the patient smokes) and plan a specific alternative for each. Breaking the meal–cigarette link by leaving the table and brushing teeth removes the cue. Allowing 'just one' or half cigarettes maintains the habit, and skipping meals is unhealthy and increases irritability.
w: Correct - changing the routine breaks the link between meals and smoking.
Wrong - skipping meals is unhealthy and does not address the habit.
Wrong - 'reward' cigarettes maintain the habit and lead to relapse.
Wrong - larger meals encourage weight gain and do not remove the cue.
Wrong - partial smoking keeps the habit going.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old man who stopped smoking 2 weeks ago is troubled by cravings in the evenings and is worried about gaining weight. He has no cardiac or joint problems.
Which behavioural advice best addresses both concerns?
o: Eat sweets whenever a craving comes on in the evening
Go to bed early so that the evening cravings are avoided
Watch television to keep his mind off the cravings
Take short bouts of exercise when cravings strike
Drink extra coffee in the evening to suppress appetite
mcq.e: Even short bouts of exercise (around 5 minutes) reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms, improve mood and help limit post-cessation weight gain. It is one of the 'divert your thinking' strategies. Sweets add calories, and coffee is a smoking cue whose levels rise after quitting.
w: Wrong - sweets add calories and worsen weight gain.
Wrong - avoids the problem without building coping skills.
Wrong - a sedentary distraction does not help weight and is often a smoking cue.
Correct - exercise reduces cravings and helps control weight.
Wrong - coffee is a smoking cue and caffeine levels rise after quitting.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old offshore oil-rig worker quit smoking 1 week ago with NRT from a Klinik Kesihatan. He works 2-week shifts at sea and cannot attend the clinic for the weekly reviews planned in his first month.
What is the most appropriate way to provide his follow-up?
o: Postpone all reviews until he returns to shore
Discharge him, as he cannot attend in person
Arrange scheduled telephone or virtual reviews
Give him 3 months of NRT and review at the end
Ask his supervisor to report whether he smokes
mcq.e: Follow-up can be in person, by telephone or virtual. Early weekly contact is important because withdrawal and relapse risk are highest in the first month. Remote reviews should still assess pharmacotherapy use and problems, congratulate success and review any lapses.
w: Wrong - delaying reviews leaves him without support at the highest-risk time.
Wrong - follow-up can be remote.
Correct - telephone or virtual follow-up is an accepted format.
Wrong - lack of early review increases relapse and misuse.
Wrong - breaches confidentiality and is not support.

mcq.stem:
A 46-year-old man who smokes 22 cigarettes a day, with his first cigarette within 10 minutes of waking, chooses nicotine patches at a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic. He has no cardiovascular disease.
What is the most appropriate starting patch strength?
o: 7 mg/24 h patch
14 mg/24 h patch
10 mg/16 h patch
15 mg/16 h patch
21 mg/24 h patch
mcq.e: Smokers of more than 10 cigarettes a day should start on the highest strength (21 mg/24 h or 25 mg/16 h), stepping down over 8–12 weeks. Heavier smokers need higher doses, and under-dosing is a common reason for NRT failure. For a highly dependent smoker, add a short-acting form for breakthrough cravings.
w: Wrong - 7 mg is the final step-down dose.
Wrong - 14 mg is the starting dose for 10 or fewer cigarettes a day.
Wrong - 10 mg/16 h is the lowest 16-hour step.
Wrong - 15 mg/16 h is for lighter smokers or step-down.
Correct - more than 10 cigarettes a day: start 21 mg/24 h.

mcq.stem:
A 39-year-old woman started a 21 mg/24-hour nicotine patch 5 days ago. Her cravings are well controlled, but she has vivid dreams and wakes several times each night. She has no skin reaction.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Remove the patch at bedtime and apply a new one on waking
Switch to the 7 mg patch strength from tonight
Stop the patch and change her treatment to bupropion
Take a sedative antihistamine each night with the patch
Move the patch to her thigh instead of her upper arm
mcq.e: Vivid dreams and sleep disturbance are common with 24-hour patches because of night-time nicotine. Removing the patch at bedtime (effectively 16-hour use) usually resolves this while keeping daytime craving control. Dropping the dose risks breakthrough withdrawal, and bupropion itself causes insomnia.
w: Correct - removing the patch at night (16-hour use) relieves vivid dreams and insomnia.
Wrong - reducing the dose risks uncontrolled cravings.
Wrong - her cravings are controlled; bupropion also commonly causes insomnia.
Wrong - adds sedation without fixing the cause.
Wrong - site does not affect night-time nicotine exposure.

mcq.stem:
A 52-year-old man started 4 mg nicotine gum 1 week ago. He chews it continuously like ordinary chewing gum and now complains of hiccups, heartburn and nausea. His cravings remain poorly controlled.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Switch to the 2 mg gum and keep chewing continuously
Chew slowly until it tingles, then park it against the cheek
Swallow the saliva promptly to absorb nicotine faster
Take an antacid and continue chewing as he does now
Chew two pieces together for about 10 minutes at a time
mcq.e: Nicotine gum works through buccal absorption. Vigorous chewing releases nicotine too fast, so it is swallowed – causing hiccups, dyspepsia and nausea – and is partly lost to first-pass metabolism, so it controls cravings poorly. The chew-and-park technique (chew until peppery or tingling, park between cheek and gum, repeat for about 30 minutes) fixes both problems.
w: Wrong - a lower dose does not fix the faulty technique.
Correct - chew-and-park allows buccal absorption and prevents swallowing.
Wrong - swallowed nicotine causes the GI side effects and is less effective.
Wrong - masks symptoms without improving absorption.
Wrong - increases nicotine release and swallowing.

mcq.stem:
A 60-year-old man was discharged 5 days ago after an acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with primary PCI. At his Klinik Kesihatan review he is determined never to smoke again but has strong cravings. He smoked 20 cigarettes a day until admission.
What is the most appropriate cessation approach now?
o: Avoid all smoking cessation medication for at least 1 year
Start a 21 mg patch with 4 mg gum without any further review
Advise cutting down to 5 a day until the heart has healed
Intensive behavioural support, with NRT only under medical supervision
Defer the quit attempt until cardiac rehabilitation has ended
mcq.e: NRT is far safer than smoking and safe in stable cardiovascular disease, but caution is advised in the acute phase – MI within about 2 weeks, unstable angina or serious arrhythmia. Prioritise intensive behavioural support and, if pharmacotherapy is needed, use NRT under medical (cardiology) supervision. Quitting after MI reduces mortality by about a third.
w: Wrong - an unnecessarily long ban; NRT is safer than smoking once stable.
Wrong - unsupervised high-dose NRT early after MI needs caution.
Wrong - any continued smoking after MI is harmful.
Correct - behavioural support first, with NRT only under medical supervision in the acute phase.
Wrong - quitting immediately gives the greatest survival benefit.

mcq.stem:
A 48-year-old man started a 21 mg/24-hour nicotine patch 3 days ago but is still smoking about 15 cigarettes a day. He presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with nausea, dizziness, headache, cold sweats and palpitations. BP 138/84 mmHg, pulse 104/min regular, ECG sinus tachycardia only.
What is the most likely cause?
o: Nicotine withdrawal from an inadequate patch dose
Nicotine excess from smoking while on a high-dose patch
Allergic reaction to the patch adhesive
Caffeine toxicity from reduced CYP1A2 activity
Viral gastroenteritis unrelated to treatment
mcq.e: Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, headache, palpitations and cold sweats suggest nicotine excess, usually from continuing to smoke heavily on high-dose NRT. Advise stopping smoking and, if symptoms persist, reducing the NRT dose. Caffeine accumulation follows quitting, which he has not done.
w: Wrong - withdrawal causes irritability and cravings, not cold sweats and nausea while still smoking.
Correct - smoking heavily on a full-strength patch causes nicotine excess.
Wrong - allergy causes local or generalised rash, not these systemic features.
Wrong - CYP1A2 induction persists because he is still smoking.
Wrong - the timing with patch plus continued smoking points to nicotine excess.

mcq.stem:
A 55-year-old man with a Fagerström score of 8 wants to quit at a Klinik Kesihatan. He prefers NRT because a friend had severe nausea on varenicline. He smokes 30 cigarettes a day and has strong cravings after meals.
Which NRT regimen is most effective?
o: 14 mg/24 h patch alone
2 mg gum alone as needed
Nicotine inhaler alone
21 mg patch plus 4 mg gum or lozenge
4 mg gum alone every 4 hours
mcq.e: Combination NRT – a long-acting patch for steady background levels plus a short-acting form for breakthrough cravings – is more effective than any single form and similar in efficacy to varenicline. It is particularly suitable for highly dependent smokers, who also need the highest patch strength.
w: Wrong - single-form and too low a dose for a 30-a-day smoker.
Wrong - low-dose, as-needed gum alone is inadequate for high dependence.
Wrong - single short-acting forms are less effective than combination therapy.
Correct - full-strength patch plus short-acting NRT is the most effective NRT regimen.
Wrong - single-form and too infrequent.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old man visits a community pharmacy in Ipoh asking to buy nicotine gum to help him stop smoking. He has no prescription and no medical problems. The pharmacist is unsure whether she can supply it.
Which statement about NRT supply in Malaysia is correct?
o: NRT is prescription-only and must be refused without one
NRT can be supplied only by a doctor at a government clinic
As a Group C poison, the pharmacist may supply it with advice
NRT is unregulated and can be sold by any retail shop
NRT may be supplied only after a doctor confirms the FTND
mcq.e: NRT products are Group C poisons under the Poisons Act 1952, so a registered pharmacist can supply them without a doctor's prescription, ideally with counselling on correct use. This improves access through community pharmacies, many of which participate in mQuit.
w: Wrong - NRT is not a prescription-only (Group B) product.
Wrong - pharmacists can supply it too.
Correct - Group C status allows pharmacist supply with counselling.
Wrong - NRT is regulated under the Poisons Act.
Wrong - an FTND is useful but not legally required.

mcq.stem:
A 68-year-old man with full upper and lower dentures and temporomandibular joint pain is starting a 21 mg nicotine patch at a Klinik Kesihatan. He also needs a short-acting NRT form for cravings after meals.
Which short-acting form is most suitable?
o: 2 mg nicotine gum
4 mg nicotine gum
Gum used with denture fixative
A second 7 mg patch after meals
Nicotine lozenge
mcq.e: Nicotine gum sticks to dentures and aggravates jaw problems. Lozenges are sucked slowly and moved around the mouth until dissolved (about 20–30 minutes), giving buccal absorption without chewing. A patch is too slow to relieve acute cravings.
w: Wrong - gum is unsuitable with dentures and TMJ pain.
Wrong - gum is unsuitable regardless of strength.
Wrong - still requires chewing and sticks to dentures.
Wrong - patches act too slowly for breakthrough cravings.
Correct - lozenges need no chewing and suit denture wearers.

mcq.stem:
A 57-year-old man using a 21 mg nicotine patch says his background cravings are controlled, but he badly misses holding a cigarette and the hand-to-mouth action, especially while driving.
Which additional NRT form best suits him?
o: Nicotine inhaler
Nicotine patch, higher dose
Nicotine lozenge
Nicotine gum
Nicotine nasal spray
mcq.e: The nicotine inhaler is a mouthpiece holding a nicotine cartridge; puffing delivers nicotine absorbed in the mouth and throat. It replaces the hand-to-mouth ritual that many smokers miss. Side effects include throat irritation and cough.
w: Correct - the inhaler mimics the hand-to-mouth behaviour of smoking.
Wrong - his background cravings are already controlled.
Wrong - helps cravings but does not replace the ritual.
Wrong - helps cravings but does not replace the ritual.
Wrong - fast-acting, but does not replace the ritual.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man on a nicotine patch admits smoking 2 cigarettes yesterday during a stressful day. He has heard that smoking while wearing a patch can cause a heart attack and wants to stop the patch.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop the patch immediately to avoid nicotine overdose
Stop the patch for 1 week and then restart it
Halve the patch strength until he stops completely
Continue the patch and recommit to stopping smoking
Switch to varenicline as NRT has clearly failed
mcq.e: Smoking a few cigarettes while using NRT is not dangerous; the belief that it causes heart attacks is a myth. Encourage him to continue NRT, recommit to abstinence, review the trigger and check the dose is adequate. Stopping NRT after a lapse raises relapse risk.
w: Wrong - an occasional cigarette on NRT does not cause dangerous overdose.
Wrong - interrupting treatment increases relapse risk.
Wrong - under-dosing worsens cravings.
Correct - continue NRT, review the trigger and recommit.
Wrong - a single stress-related lapse does not mean failure.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man with COPD who smokes 25 cigarettes a day tells the Klinik Kesihatan doctor he cannot face stopping abruptly but would like to smoke less. He has declined to set a quit date today.
What is the most appropriate pharmacological approach?
o: Use NRT to cut down, then set a quit date
Offer no medication until he sets a quit date
Start varenicline with no planned quit date
Advise switching to e-cigarettes to cut down
Use nicotine gum only on days he smokes less
mcq.e: For smokers not ready to stop completely, NRT can be used to reduce cigarette intake before quitting ('cut down to quit'), with the aim of setting a quit date as confidence grows. Smoking while using NRT is not dangerous. This keeps the patient engaged rather than turning him away.
w: Correct - NRT can be used to reduce intake before a planned quit.
Wrong - NRT is licensed to help smokers cut down before quitting.
Wrong - varenicline is started 1–2 weeks before a set quit date.
Wrong - e-cigarettes are not an approved cessation aid in Malaysia.
Wrong - irregular use is ineffective; regular NRT should replace cigarettes.

mcq.stem:
A 44-year-old man with normal renal function is starting varenicline at a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic. His quit date is set for day 8 of treatment.
Which dosing schedule is correct?
o: 0.5 mg BD for 3 days, 1 mg OD for 4 days, then 1 mg BD
1 mg OD for 3 days, 1 mg BD for 4 days, then 2 mg BD
0.5 mg OD for 7 days, then 1 mg OD for the rest
1 mg BD from day 1 for a total of 12 weeks
0.5 mg OD for 3 days, 0.5 mg BD for 4 days, then 1 mg BD
mcq.e: Varenicline is titrated to reduce nausea: 0.5 mg once daily on days 1–3, 0.5 mg twice daily on days 4–7, then 1 mg twice daily from day 8 to complete 12 weeks. The quit date is usually between day 8 and day 14.
w: Wrong - the titration starts at 0.5 mg once daily.
Wrong - doses are too high; the maximum is 1 mg twice daily.
Wrong - the maintenance dose is 1 mg twice daily.
Wrong - starting at full dose increases nausea.
Correct - 0.5 mg OD days 1–3, 0.5 mg BD days 4–7, then 1 mg BD.

mcq.stem:
A 37-year-old woman started varenicline 5 days ago. She has troublesome nausea, especially in the mornings, but no vomiting. Her mood is normal, and she is keen to continue because cigarettes already taste less satisfying.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop varenicline and switch to bupropion SR
Take it on an empty stomach for faster absorption
Take it after food with a full glass of water
Double the dose to speed up tolerance to nausea
Stop varenicline for 1 week and then restart
mcq.e: Nausea is the commonest adverse effect of varenicline (about 3 in 10 patients), is usually mild and often settles. Taking it after food with a full glass of water reduces it; if persistent, the dose can be reduced. Stopping or switching is not needed for mild nausea.
w: Wrong - mild nausea does not require a change of drug.
Wrong - an empty stomach worsens nausea.
Correct - taking varenicline after food with water reduces nausea.
Wrong - a higher dose worsens nausea.
Wrong - interruption risks relapse and is unnecessary.

mcq.stem:
A 32-year-old man on week 4 of varenicline is brought by his wife to a Klinik Kesihatan. Over the past week he has become withdrawn, tearful and irritable, and said he 'might be better off dead'. He has not smoked since his quit date.
What is the most appropriate immediate action regarding varenicline?
o: Continue varenicline and review him in 4 weeks
Stop varenicline now and assess and manage his mood urgently
Halve the varenicline dose and add an antidepressant
Continue varenicline, as this is nicotine withdrawal
Switch from varenicline to bupropion SR the same day
mcq.e: Serious adverse effects listed for varenicline include depression, suicidal ideation and suicide. If mood or behaviour changes, varenicline should be stopped and the patient assessed immediately – including a suicide risk assessment and referral as needed. Although large trials did not show a significant excess risk, a patient with suicidal ideation must be managed urgently.
w: Wrong - suicidal ideation needs immediate action, not routine review.
Correct - stop varenicline and assess mood and suicide risk urgently.
Wrong - continuing the drug with suicidal ideation is unsafe.
Wrong - suicidal thoughts must not be dismissed as withdrawal.
Wrong - bupropion also carries neuropsychiatric warnings; his mood needs assessment first.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old lorry driver attends the quit smoking clinic at a Klinik Kesihatan. He smokes 25 cigarettes a day and his Fagerström score is 7. He has epilepsy, controlled on sodium valproate, with his last seizure 3 years ago. He failed a previous quit attempt with nicotine gum alone and asks for a stronger medicine.
Which of the following should be AVOIDED in him?
o: Bupropion SR 150 mg
Varenicline tartrate
Nicotine patch 21 mg/24 h
Nicotine gum 4 mg
Nicotine lozenge 4 mg
mcq.e: Bupropion lowers the seizure threshold and is contraindicated in anyone with a current or past seizure disorder, however well controlled. Varenicline and all forms of NRT remain options; combination NRT (patch plus a short-acting form) or varenicline would suit his high dependence. The trap is assuming that a seizure-free epilepsy no longer counts.
w: Correct - a history of seizures is an absolute contraindication to bupropion.
Wrong - varenicline is not contraindicated in epilepsy and suits a highly dependent smoker.
Wrong - the nicotine patch is safe in epilepsy and is the backbone of combination NRT.
Wrong - 4 mg gum is appropriate for high dependence and can be combined with a patch.
Wrong - lozenges are a safe short-acting NRT option in epilepsy.

mcq.stem:
A 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan. His latest creatinine clearance is 24 mL/min. He smokes 20 cigarettes a day and, after counselling, chooses varenicline. He is not on dialysis.
Which varenicline regimen is most appropriate?
o: Standard titration up to 1 mg twice daily
Start 0.5 mg daily, max 0.5 mg twice daily
Start 1 mg daily, maximum 1 mg twice daily
Give 0.5 mg on alternate days throughout
Standard titration, then stop after 4 weeks
mcq.e: Varenicline is excreted largely unchanged by the kidneys, so severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30 mL/min) needs a lower dose: start 0.5 mg once daily and titrate to a maximum of 0.5 mg twice daily. It is not contraindicated, and shortening the course is not the way to reduce exposure – the full 12 weeks is still given.
w: Wrong - full dosing in severe renal impairment risks accumulation and adverse effects.
Correct - CrCl below 30 mL/min: 0.5 mg daily, up to a maximum of 0.5 mg twice daily.
Wrong - this is higher than the usual starting dose and unsafe in severe renal impairment.
Wrong - alternate-day dosing is not a recommended regimen and is likely sub-therapeutic.
Wrong - the course length stays at 12 weeks; it is the dose that is reduced.

mcq.stem:
A 40-year-old teacher who smokes 18 cigarettes a day is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic. She chooses to set her quit date on the first day of the school holidays, which is 10 days from today, and she is prescribed varenicline.
When should she take her first dose of varenicline?
o: On the morning of her quit date
Only after she has been abstinent for 1 week
Today, so she starts 1-2 weeks before quitting
Four weeks before her chosen quit date
Only when strong cravings appear after quitting
mcq.e: Varenicline needs about a week of titration (0.5 mg daily for 3 days, 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days, then 1 mg twice daily) to reach steady state, so it is started 1-2 weeks before the quit date. Starting on the quit day leaves her under-treated during peak withdrawal. Unlike NRT, it is not used 'as needed' for cravings.
w: Wrong - this gives no time for titration, so withdrawal peaks before the drug is effective.
Wrong - waiting for abstinence removes the support she needs during early withdrawal.
Correct - start 1-2 weeks before the quit date so the full dose is reached by quit day.
Wrong - starting a month ahead is unnecessary and adds side effects without benefit.
Wrong - varenicline is a fixed scheduled course, not an as-needed craving treatment.

mcq.stem:
A 58-year-old man is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan 6 weeks after an ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with primary PCI. He has occasional ventricular ectopics on his ECG. He has restarted smoking 10 cigarettes a day and wants help to stop. The doctor reviews the options.
Which pharmacotherapy is contraindicated in him at this stage?
o: Nicotine patch 14 mg/24 h
Varenicline titrated over a week
Bupropion SR 150 mg
Nortriptyline started at 25 mg
Nicotine gum 2 mg as needed
mcq.e: Nortriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant and is contraindicated in the recovery period after a myocardial infarction and in arrhythmias because of its pro-arrhythmic, conduction-slowing effects. NRT is far safer than continued smoking once the patient is stable (caution only in the first 2 weeks or with unstable angina), and varenicline and bupropion are not contraindicated after MI.
w: Wrong - NRT is safer than smoking in stable cardiac disease beyond the acute period.
Wrong - varenicline is not contraindicated after MI; trials showed no clear excess of cardiac events.
Wrong - bupropion is not contraindicated after MI, though blood pressure should be monitored.
Correct - tricyclics are contraindicated after recent MI and in arrhythmia.
Wrong - short-acting NRT can be used in stable patients after MI.

mcq.stem:
A 35-year-old man has been taking bupropion SR 150 mg twice daily for 10 days. He takes his doses at 8 am and 10 pm. He has not smoked for 3 days but now complains of difficulty falling asleep every night. He has no other side effects and wants to continue treatment.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Take both tablets together at bedtime
Add a nightly benzodiazepine for 4 weeks
Stop bupropion and start nortriptyline
Increase to 150 mg three times daily
Take the second dose in the afternoon
mcq.e: Insomnia is one of the commonest adverse effects of bupropion. It is minimised by taking the second dose earlier in the day (for example mid-afternoon), keeping the doses at least 8 hours apart and avoiding a bedtime dose. Doubling up a single dose raises the seizure risk, and benzodiazepines add dependence and, on withdrawal, seizure risk.
w: Wrong - a single 300 mg dose raises the seizure risk and worsens insomnia.
Wrong - benzodiazepines add dependence, and their withdrawal lowers the seizure threshold on bupropion.
Wrong - a manageable side effect does not require switching to a second-line drug.
Wrong - the maximum dose is 300 mg/day; more doses would worsen insomnia and seizure risk.
Correct - move the second dose earlier, at least 8 hours after the first, avoiding bedtime.

mcq.stem:
A 26-year-old woman, G2P1 at 10 weeks of gestation, attends her booking visit at a Klinik Kesihatan. She smokes 8 cigarettes a day and her husband also smokes at home. She says she wants to stop for the baby but has never tried before.
What is the most appropriate first step?
o: Multi-session behavioural support
Start a 21 mg 24-hour nicotine patch
Varenicline from the second trimester
Bupropion SR after the first trimester
Cut down to 5 cigarettes a day for now
mcq.e: All pregnant and breastfeeding women who smoke should be offered multi-session behavioural cessation support as first-line, ideally at every antenatal visit and including the partner. NRT is considered only if behavioural support alone fails. Varenicline, bupropion and nortriptyline are not used in pregnancy, and 'cutting down' is not a safe target.
w: Correct - multi-session behavioural support is first-line for every pregnant smoker.
Wrong - NRT is second step if behavioural support fails, and intermittent short-acting forms are preferred.
Wrong - varenicline cannot be used in pregnancy at any stage.
Wrong - bupropion cannot be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding.
Wrong - cutting down still exposes the fetus; complete cessation is the goal.

mcq.stem:
A 38-year-old man with schizophrenia, stable for 2 years on clozapine 400 mg daily, stopped smoking 20 cigarettes a day 10 days ago using a nicotine patch. His mother brings him to a Klinik Kesihatan because he is very drowsy, drooling and has had brief jerks of his arms.
What is the most likely mechanism of his symptoms?
o: Nicotine from the patch blocking clozapine breakdown
Loss of CYP1A2 induction by tobacco smoke
Nicotine withdrawal causing central sedation
Reduced renal clearance of clozapine after quitting
Dopamine surge caused by the nicotine patch
mcq.e: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke – not nicotine – induce hepatic CYP1A2, which metabolises clozapine and olanzapine. When a patient stops smoking the induction wears off over about a week, clozapine levels rise sharply and toxicity (sedation, hypersalivation, myoclonus, seizures) follows. NRT does not prevent this; the dose must be reduced with level monitoring in liaison with psychiatry.
w: Wrong - nicotine itself neither induces nor inhibits CYP1A2, so the patch is not the cause.
Correct - smoke hydrocarbons induce CYP1A2; on quitting, clozapine levels rise to toxic levels.
Wrong - withdrawal causes irritability and insomnia, not drooling and myoclonus.
Wrong - clozapine is cleared mainly by hepatic metabolism, not the kidneys.
Wrong - this is drug toxicity from raised clozapine levels, not a nicotine effect.

mcq.stem:
A 16-year-old boy is brought to a Klinik Kesihatan by his mother, who found cigarettes in his school bag. He smokes about 4 cigarettes a day with friends after school, has his first cigarette in the afternoon and has no withdrawal symptoms when he cannot smoke. He says he would like to stop.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Counselling and behavioural support
A 12-week course of varenicline
Bupropion SR 1 week before quitting
Nortriptyline at a low starting dose
Combination nicotine patch and gum
mcq.e: Counselling and behavioural interventions are first-line for adolescent smokers. Pharmacotherapy is considered only when there is clear nicotine dependence plus a desire to quit, and he has low dependence (late first cigarette, no withdrawal). Varenicline and nortriptyline are not for under-18s; NRT is the usual option if medication is later needed.
w: Wrong - this boy shows low dependence; varenicline is also not licensed under 18.
Wrong - drug treatment is not indicated with low dependence, and bupropion is not for under-18s per slide p49.
Correct - counselling and behavioural support are first-line in adolescents.
Wrong - nortriptyline is not recommended under 18 years.
Wrong - NRT is kept for adolescents with evidence of nicotine dependence.

mcq.stem:
A 20-year-old college student presents to a Klinik Kesihatan with 5 days of dry cough, breathlessness, pleuritic chest pain, nausea and vomiting. For the past 2 months he has used a refillable pod device with cannabis oil cartridges bought online. Temperature 38.2 °C, RR 26/min, SpO2 91% on air. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hazy infiltrates. COVID-19 and influenza rapid tests are negative and he has no TB contact.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Atypical community-acquired pneumonia
Pulmonary tuberculosis with cavitation
Acute severe asthma exacerbation
Vaping product-associated lung injury
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax
mcq.e: EVALI presents in young vapers (especially of THC products containing vitamin E acetate) with respiratory symptoms plus prominent GI symptoms and fever, hypoxia and bilateral infiltrates, with infection excluded. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: e-cigarette use within 90 days, pulmonary infiltrates and no other plausible cause. He needs urgent hospital referral given hypoxia.
w: Wrong - pneumonia must be excluded, but GI symptoms, THC vaping and bilateral infiltrates point to EVALI.
Wrong - 5 days of illness without TB contact or cavitation does not fit tuberculosis.
Wrong - asthma causes wheeze with a clear chest X-ray, not bilateral infiltrates.
Correct - vaping within 90 days, bilateral infiltrates and no other cause define EVALI.
Wrong - pneumothorax gives a visible lung edge on X-ray, not bilateral infiltrates or fever.

mcq.stem:
A 45-year-old man who smokes 20 cigarettes a day attends a Klinik Kesihatan for a hypertension review. He is ready to quit and says his colleague stopped smoking by switching to vaping. He asks whether he should do the same.
What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Switch fully to vaping, then taper the nicotine
Vape alongside cigarettes to cut down gradually
Use a heated tobacco device as a safer bridge
Use nicotine-free vape liquid to stay safe
Use NRT or varenicline with behavioural support
mcq.e: E-cigarettes are not an approved smoking cessation therapy in Malaysia and are not recommended in the MOH CPG. Many users end up as dual users, maintaining nicotine dependence and harm. He should be offered evidence-based treatment: behavioural support plus NRT (ideally combination) or varenicline, with referral to a quit clinic or mQuit services.
w: Wrong - e-cigarettes are not an approved cessation aid in Malaysia and carry their own harms.
Wrong - dual use maintains dependence and does not reduce cardiovascular harm meaningfully.
Wrong - heated tobacco products still deliver nicotine and toxicants and are not recommended.
Wrong - nicotine-free liquids still contain propylene glycol, flavourings and toxicants.
Correct - offer evidence-based pharmacotherapy plus behavioural support.

mcq.stem:
A 22-year-old university student wants to stop smoking 15 cigarettes a day and asks for bupropion because she read it limits weight gain. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill, uses a salbutamol inhaler for mild asthma and drinks 2 cups of coffee daily. On further questioning she binges and then induces vomiting about three times a week. BMI is 20 kg/m².
Which feature of her history makes bupropion inappropriate?
o: Use of the combined oral contraceptive pill
Mild asthma treated with salbutamol
Binge eating with self-induced vomiting
Drinking 2 cups of coffee every day
Her age, being under 25 years old
mcq.e: Bupropion is contraindicated in current or past bulimia or anorexia nervosa because of a higher seizure risk (electrolyte disturbance plus the drug's lowering of the seizure threshold). Her request for help with weight should prompt screening for an eating disorder. Varenicline or NRT are suitable alternatives, and the eating disorder needs its own management.
w: Wrong - oral contraceptives are not a contraindication to bupropion.
Wrong - asthma and salbutamol do not preclude bupropion.
Correct - bulimia or anorexia nervosa is a contraindication because of seizure risk.
Wrong - moderate caffeine intake is not a contraindication.
Wrong - bupropion is restricted under 18 years, not under 25.

mcq.stem:
A 50-year-old man is on week 4 of varenicline and stopped smoking on his quit date. At follow-up in a Klinik Kesihatan he admits he smoked one cigarette at a wedding but says it 'did nothing for him' and he did not want another. He asks why.
Which mechanism best explains his experience?
o: Partial agonism blocking nicotine at α4β2 receptors
Inhibition of hepatic CYP2A6 metabolism of nicotine
Blockade of dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum
Induction of enzymes that clear nicotine faster
Full agonism that saturates nicotinic receptors
mcq.e: Varenicline is a partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors. Its agonist action maintains moderate dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens to ease withdrawal, while its antagonist action occupies the receptors so nicotine from a cigarette cannot produce its usual reward – hence reduced smoking satisfaction. This dual action explains why a lapse on varenicline is less likely to become a full relapse.
w: Correct - as a partial agonist it occupies α4β2 receptors and blunts nicotine's reward.
Wrong - inhibiting nicotine metabolism would raise nicotine levels, not reduce satisfaction.
