Wrong - varenicline does not block dopamine receptors; it modulates dopamine release.
Wrong - varenicline is not an enzyme inducer and has few metabolic interactions.
Wrong - it is a partial, not full, agonist; full agonism would mimic smoking.

mcq.stem:
A 47-year-old woman has just completed a 12-week course of varenicline and has not smoked for 11 weeks, confirmed by a low exhaled carbon monoxide reading. She tolerated the drug well but is very worried about relapsing, as her two previous attempts failed at about 3 months.
What is the most appropriate management?
o: Stop varenicline and start bupropion SR
Switch to a 21 mg nicotine patch for 12 weeks
Stop varenicline and discharge from clinic
Increase varenicline to 2 mg twice daily
Offer a further 12 weeks of varenicline
mcq.e: For smokers who have successfully quit on varenicline, an additional 12-week course increases long-term abstinence and is recommended for those at risk of relapse. Continuing a drug she tolerates is better than switching to an unproven sequence, and the maximum dose is 1 mg twice daily. Behavioural follow-up should continue alongside.
w: Wrong - switching drugs in an abstinent patient has no evidence of extra benefit.
Wrong - a full-strength patch re-exposes an abstinent patient to nicotine without need.
Wrong - she is at high relapse risk and benefits from continued treatment and follow-up.
Wrong - the maximum varenicline dose is 1 mg twice daily.
Correct - a further 12 weeks of varenicline reduces relapse in those who have quit.

mcq.stem:
A 41-year-old man with no seizure history, no eating disorder and normal liver and kidney function chooses bupropion SR to help him stop smoking. He sets a quit date 8 days from today. He drinks no alcohol and takes no regular medicines.
Which regimen is correct?
o: 300 mg once daily from day 1, for 4 weeks
150 mg twice daily from day 1, for 6 months
75 mg daily for 1 week, then 150 mg daily, for 6 weeks
150 mg daily for 3 days, then BD, for 7-12 weeks
0.5 mg daily for 3 days, then 1 mg BD, for 12 weeks
mcq.e: Bupropion SR is started 1-2 weeks before the quit date at 150 mg once daily for 3 days, then 150 mg twice daily (at least 8 hours apart), to a maximum of 300 mg/day. The slides advise at least 7 weeks of use; 7-12 weeks is standard. A single 300 mg dose raises seizure risk, and the 0.5 mg/1 mg schedule belongs to varenicline.
w: Wrong - a single 300 mg dose raises the seizure risk and the course is too short.
Wrong - bupropion is titrated up, and 6 months exceeds the usual course.
Wrong - 150 mg daily alone is a reduced dose reserved for hepatic, renal or seizure risk.
Correct - 150 mg daily for 3 days, then 150 mg twice daily for 7-12 weeks.
Wrong - this is the varenicline titration schedule, not bupropion.

mcq.stem:
A 30-year-old woman at 24 weeks of gestation has attended four behavioural support sessions at a Klinik Kesihatan quit clinic. She has cut down from 15 to 10 cigarettes a day but cannot stop completely and remains keen to quit. Her pregnancy is otherwise uncomplicated.
What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Varenicline after counselling on risks
Short-acting NRT such as gum or lozenge
Bupropion SR from 1 week before quitting
21 mg patch worn day and night
Nortriptyline at the lowest effective dose
mcq.e: If behavioural support alone fails in pregnancy, NRT may be used after discussing risks and benefits, because it is safer than continued smoking. Intermittent short-acting forms (gum, lozenge, inhaler, spray) are preferred to limit total fetal nicotine exposure; if a patch is used it should be removed at bedtime. Varenicline, bupropion and nortriptyline are not used in pregnancy.
w: Wrong - varenicline cannot be used in pregnancy.
Correct - intermittent short-acting NRT is preferred when behavioural support alone fails.
Wrong - bupropion cannot be used in pregnant or breastfeeding women.
Wrong - continuous 24-hour patches maximise fetal exposure; remove a patch at bedtime.
Wrong - nortriptyline is not recommended in pregnancy.

mcq.stem:
A 34-year-old woman with bipolar disorder stopped her lithium 3 weeks ago. Her sister brings her to a Klinik Kesihatan because she has slept 2-3 hours a night for 5 days, is talking rapidly and has spent her savings. She smokes 30 cigarettes a day and says she wants to quit smoking today.
What is the most appropriate approach to her smoking?
o: Start varenicline today with weekly review
Treat mood first, set quit date once stable
Set the quit date for tomorrow with NRT
Advise that she should never try to quit
Start bupropion SR to treat mood and smoking
mcq.e: In psychiatric patients the quit date should be set when the mental state is stable. She has features of acute mania and needs urgent psychiatric management first; her smoking status should be recorded and cessation offered once stable, with pharmacotherapy and behavioural support. Smokers with mental illness should still be supported to quit – they gain mental as well as physical benefit.
w: Wrong - starting varenicline during acute mania is inappropriate; stabilise her first.
Correct - manage the manic episode urgently and set the quit date once her mental state is stable.
Wrong - a quit attempt during acute mania is unlikely to succeed and distracts from urgent care.
Wrong - people with mental illness should be offered full cessation support when stable.
Wrong - bupropion is an antidepressant and may worsen mania; it does not treat bipolar disorder.

mcq.stem:
A 74-year-old retired fisherman with hypertension and stable ischaemic heart disease is seen at a Klinik Kesihatan. He has smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 55 years. When advised to quit he says, 'At my age the damage is done, there is no point stopping now.'
Which response is most accurate?
o: Quitting still lowers his cardiac and death risk
Agree, as quitting gives little benefit after 70
Advise cutting down to 10 a day as a safer target
Advise switching to vaping to protect his heart
Advise quitting only if new heart symptoms occur
mcq.e: Stopping smoking reduces the excess risk of cardiovascular events and mortality even in older people, and NRT increases cessation success in this group. Counselling, physician advice, buddy support, age-tailored self-help materials, telephone counselling and the nicotine patch are all effective in the elderly. Age is never a reason to withhold cessation support.
w: Correct - quitting reduces cardiovascular events and mortality even at older age.
Wrong - benefit persists at any age; this reinforces a common misconception.
Wrong - cutting down gives little risk reduction; complete cessation is the aim.
Wrong - e-cigarettes are not an approved cessation aid in Malaysia.
Wrong - waiting for symptoms forfeits the preventive benefit of quitting now.

mcq.stem:
A 28-year-old woman is 6 weeks postpartum and exclusively breastfeeding. She stopped smoking in pregnancy but relapsed to 10 cigarettes a day after delivery. She has attended behavioural support sessions but is still smoking and asks for medication to help her stop.
Which option is most appropriate?
o: Varenicline, as little enters breast milk
Bupropion SR with no night-time feeds
Nortriptyline at a low dose at bedtime
Stop breastfeeding, then use varenicline
Short-acting NRT used just after feeds
mcq.e: Varenicline, bupropion and nortriptyline are not used in breastfeeding women, so NRT is the pharmacological option when behavioural support alone fails. Using short-acting NRT immediately after a feed minimises nicotine in the milk at the next feed. Breastfeeding should be supported, not stopped, to allow a drug.
w: Wrong - varenicline cannot be used in breastfeeding women.
Wrong - bupropion cannot be used while breastfeeding, whatever the feeding pattern.
Wrong - nortriptyline is not recommended in breastfeeding women.
Wrong - stopping breastfeeding harms the infant and is unnecessary when NRT is available.
Correct - short-acting NRT taken just after a feed limits infant exposure.

mcq.stem:
A 2-year-old boy is rushed to a Klinik Kesihatan 30 minutes after he was found chewing his father's open e-liquid refill bottle. He has vomited three times and is pale, sweaty and drooling. Heart rate is 170/min and he is irritable and tremulous.
Which component of the e-liquid is most likely responsible?
o: Propylene glycol base
Vegetable glycerol base
Concentrated nicotine
Flavouring chemicals
Vitamin E acetate
mcq.e: Accidental nicotine overdose is a recognised hazard of e-cigarettes, and refill liquids can contain enough nicotine to poison a small child. Early nicotine toxicity is cholinergic: vomiting, pallor, sweating, salivation, tachycardia and tremor, progressing to seizures, bradycardia and respiratory failure. He needs urgent transfer to hospital. Vitamin E acetate causes lung injury when inhaled, not acute poisoning on ingestion.
w: Wrong - propylene glycol is of low acute toxicity in small ingestions.
Wrong - glycerol is of low toxicity and does not cause cholinergic features.
Correct - concentrated nicotine causes vomiting, sweating, salivation and tachycardia in children.
Wrong - flavourings are an inhalational concern, not the cause of acute cholinergic toxicity.
Wrong - vitamin E acetate is linked to inhaled lung injury (EVALI), not ingestion poisoning.

mcq.stem:
A 23-year-old man is referred from a Klinik Kesihatan with 3 weeks of cough, breathlessness and weight loss. Chest CT shows bilateral ground-glass opacities, and blood and sputum cultures, respiratory viral PCR and sputum AFB are negative. The team considers e-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury.
Besides pulmonary infiltrates and no other plausible cause, which criterion is required by the case definition?
o: Fever above 38 °C at presentation
Positive urine test for cannabis (THC)
Bilateral pleural effusions on imaging
Vaping within 90 days of symptom onset
Vaping history of at least 12 months
mcq.e: The EVALI case definition used in the 2019 US outbreak requires e-cigarette use within 90 days of symptom onset, pulmonary infiltrates on imaging, and no other plausible cause after excluding infection. Fever and THC use are common but not required, and there is no minimum duration of vaping.
w: Wrong - fever is common in EVALI but is not part of the case definition.
Wrong - THC products are strongly linked, but a positive test is not required.
Wrong - pleural effusions are not a defining feature; infiltrates are.
Correct - e-cigarette use within 90 days before symptom onset is required.
Wrong - there is no minimum vaping duration; recent use within 90 days is what counts.
